vignette: A 68-year-old man presents to your clinic with a 3-month history of severe burning pain on the left side of his chest. He had a vesicular rash in the same area 4 months ago that has since healed. The pain is constant, rated 7/10, and is accompanied by extreme sensitivity to touch in the affected area. He describes even light clothing as painful. He has tried acetaminophen with minimal relief. His medical history includes well-controlled hypertension. Physical examination reveals an area of healed skin with some scarring in a T5 dermatome distribution on the left.
stem: Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis? Select 1 or select "None" if none is indicated.
explanation: This patient has classic postherpetic neuralgia (PHN). The key diagnostic features include:

History of vesicular rash (herpes zoster) 4 months ago Persistent pain continuing beyond healing of the rash (>3 months) Dermatomal distribution (T5) Burning pain quality Allodynia (pain from non-noxious stimuli - light touch) Location in thoracic dermatome (50% of herpes zoster cases affect thoracic dermatomes) Postherpetic neuralgia is defined as pain persisting after the acute herpes zoster infection has resolved. The risk increases with age and severity of the eruption.
Why other options are incorrect:
Option 1 (Acute herpes zoster): The rash has healed and the pain has persisted for 3 months after rash resolution. This is chronic, not acute.

Option 3 (Intercostal neuralgia): While this could cause chest wall pain, there is no history of trauma or other cause, and the clear temporal relationship with herpes zoster makes PHN the correct diagnosis.
Option 4 (Cardiac angina): Angina is not associated with skin sensitivity, does not have a dermatomal distribution, and typically relates to exertion rather than being constant.
Option 5 (Diabetic neuropathy): Patient has no history of diabetes, and diabetic neuropathy typically presents in a stocking-glove distribution, not dermatomal.

vignette: A 72-year-old woman with postherpetic neuralgia has been experiencing severe burning pain for 6 months following an episode of herpes zoster on her right forehead. She rates her pain as 8/10. She has tried gabapentin 900 mg three times daily with some improvement but continues to have significant pain and the sedation is limiting her daily activities. You decide to start a tricyclic antidepressant.
stem: Which one of the following would be the most appropriate initial dose and medication to prescribe? Select 1 or select "None" if none is indicated.
explanation: Tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs) are first-line agents for chronic peripheral neuropathic pain, including postherpetic neuralgia. The appropriate approach is to "start low, go slow":

Initial dose: 10-25 mg at bedtime Increase by 10-25 mg at weekly intervals Titrate until pain relief or side effects occur Amitriptyline 10 mg at bedtime represents the correct starting dose for this elderly patient. Starting at a low dose minimizes side effects (dry mouth, constipation, drowsiness, urinary retention, confusion, cardiac effects) which are particularly important in elderly patients.
Why other options are incorrect:

Option 1 (Amitriptyline 75 mg at bedtime): This dose is too high to start with in an elderly patient. The risk of side effects (especially confusion, falls, anticholinergic effects) would be unacceptable. This might be a target dose after gradual titration.

Option 3 (Nortriptyline 50 mg at bedtime): While nortriptyline is an appropriate TCA choice (may have fewer anticholinergic side effects than amitriptyline), 50 mg is too high as a starting dose. Should start at 10-25 mg.
Option 4 (Desipramine 100 mg at bedtime): Desipramine is another appropriate TCA, but 100 mg is far too high as a starting dose.

Option 5 (Fluoxetine 20 mg daily): Fluoxetine is an SSRI, not a TCA. SSRIs are not effective for neuropathic pain. TCAs and SNRIs (duloxetine, venlafaxine) are the antidepressants with evidence for neuropathic pain.

vignette: A 62-year-old woman presents with right-sided facial pain for the past 2 months. She describes sudden, electric shock-like pains lasting seconds, occurring multiple times daily. The pain is triggered by touching her right cheek near her nose, chewing, and talking. The pain is confined to her right upper lip and cheek area. She has no rash and no sensory loss. Physical examination is unremarkable except for a trigger zone in the right nasolabial area. Neurological examination is otherwise normal.
stem: Which one of the following is the most appropriate first-line medication? Select 1 or select "None" if none is indicated.
explanation: This patient has classic trigeminal neuralgia (tic douloureux). The diagnostic features include:

Electric shock-like quality of pain Brief duration (seconds) Trigger zones (nasolabial region) Triggered by tactile stimuli (touching, chewing, talking) Confined to trigeminal distribution (second division in this case) Unilateral Patient over 50 years old Carbamazepine is the first-line treatment for trigeminal neuralgia and is highly effective for this specific condition. It is generally NOT effective for other types of neuropathic pain unless there is a shock-like component. The appropriate starting dose is 100 mg BID-QID, increased by 100 mg daily at weekly intervals until good pain control or intolerable side effects.
Why other options are incorrect:

Option 1 (Amitriptyline): While TCAs are first-line for most chronic peripheral neuropathic pain conditions (e.g., postherpetic neuralgia, diabetic neuropathy), they are inferior to carbamazepine for trigeminal neuralgia.
Option 2 (Gabapentin): GABA derivatives are first-line for general neuropathic pain but are not as effective as carbamazepine for trigeminal neuralgia. Gabapentin may be tried if carbamazepine fails.
Option 4 (Morphine): Opioids are third-line agents for neuropathic pain and should not be used as first-line therapy. Carbamazepine is highly effective for trigeminal neuralgia.
Option 5 (Topical lidocaine): Topical agents are not appropriate for trigeminal neuralgia, which requires systemic therapy.

vignette: A 58-year-old man with diabetic peripheral neuropathy has been taking gabapentin 1800 mg/day (600 mg three times daily) for the past 2 months with good pain relief. However, he is experiencing significant sedation and dizziness that is interfering with his work. You decide to switch him to pregabalin.
stem: Which one of the following is the most appropriate initial dosing regimen for pregabalin? Select 1 or select "None" if none is indicated.
explanation: When switching from gabapentin to pregabalin, it's important to start pregabalin at an appropriate dose and titrate gradually. Pregabalin dosing guidelines:

Initial: 50-150 mg/day in 2 divided doses Increase dose weekly by 50-150 mg/day Usual effective dose: 300-600 mg/day Maximum: 600 mg/day Pregabalin 75 mg twice daily (150 mg/day total) represents a reasonable starting dose. Key advantages of pregabalin over gabapentin:

BID dosing (vs TID for gabapentin) More predictable pharmacokinetics May have better tolerability in some patients The patient should be monitored for efficacy and side effects, with gradual dose increases if needed.
Why other options are incorrect:
Option 1 (600 mg once daily): This is the maximum daily dose and should never be given once daily. Pregabalin is dosed BID, not once daily. This would likely cause severe side effects.

Option 2 (300 mg twice daily): This is the upper end of the usual effective dose range (600 mg/day total). Starting at this high dose would likely reproduce the sedation problems and is not appropriate initial dosing.
Option 4 (150 mg TID): Pregabalin is dosed BID, not TID. One of its advantages over gabapentin is twice-daily dosing.

Option 5 (50 mg once daily): While 50 mg is at the lower end of the starting dose range, it should be given in divided doses (BID), not once daily. Also, 50 mg/day total is likely too low to provide adequate pain relief.

vignette: A 75-year-old man with Parkinson disease develops visual hallucinations but remains calm and not distressed. Family is concerned.

explanation: MAO-B inhibitors interact with dextromethorphan, meperidine, sympathomimetics, SSRIs, TCAs, and MAO-A inhibitors due to risk of serotonin syndrome or hypertensive crisis.

vignette: A 61-year-old man abruptly stops his levodopa due to nausea and presents with fever, rigidity, and confusion.
stem: Which statements are correct?

options.text: It is caused by abrupt dopaminergic withdrawal
Drug holidays are recommended to prevent dyskinesia
Dopaminergic therapy should be restarted promptly
Hyponatremia may be a risk factor

explanation: Abrupt withdrawal of dopaminergic therapy can precipitate parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia syndrome, which is clinically indistinguishable from neuroleptic malignant syndrome (fever, rigidity, autonomic instability, altered consciousness, raised CK).
Management is prompt reinstatement of dopaminergic therapy plus supportive care.
Drug holidays are NOT recommended — they are precisely what precipitates this syndrome.

vignette: A 45-year-old woman with chronic neuropathic pain from a traumatic nerve injury has been stable on morphine controlled-release 60 mg twice daily for the past 6 months with good pain control. She now reports breakthrough pain occurring 2-3 times per day, each lasting about 30 minutes. She asks about rescue medication for these episodes.
stem: Which one of the following would be the most appropriate rescue dose of morphine for breakthrough pain? Select 1 or select "None" if none is indicated.

options.text: Increase morphine controlled-release to 90 mg twice daily

explanation: For breakthrough pain in patients on sustained-release opioids, the appropriate rescue dose of immediate-release opioid is typically 10% of the total daily dose, given as needed.
Calculation:

Current total daily dose: 60 mg BID = 120 mg/day 10% of total daily dose: 120 mg × 0.10 = 12 mg Therefore: Morphine immediate-release 12 mg PRN for breakthrough pain This allows the patient to manage breakthrough pain episodes while maintaining the baseline controlled-release regimen. If she requires frequent rescue doses (more than 2-3 per day regularly), the baseline controlled-release dose should be increased.
Why other options are incorrect:
Option 1 (5 mg PRN): This is too low. It represents only about 4% of the total daily dose and is unlikely to provide adequate relief for breakthrough pain.
Option 3 (30 mg PRN): This is too high (25% of total daily dose) and could lead to excessive sedation and respiratory depression.
Option 4 (60 mg PRN): This is equal to a single dose of the controlled-release formulation and is far too high for rescue dosing. This could cause serious adverse effects.

Option 5 (Increase controlled-release to 90 mg BID): While increasing the baseline dose might be appropriate if breakthrough pain is frequent, the question specifically asks about rescue medication. Also, you would want to assess the frequency and pattern of breakthrough pain before increasing baseline dose.

vignette: A patient with trigeminal neuralgia is being started on carbamazepine.
stem: Which of the following monitoring parameters should be assessed during the first 3 months of therapy? Select 3 or select "None" if none apply.
explanation: Carbamazepine requires specific monitoring during initiation of therapy to detect rare but serious idiosyncratic reactions:
Required monitoring (first 3 months):

Complete blood count (CBC) (Option 2): To detect bone marrow suppression (rare but serious) - check every 1-2 weeks during first 3 months ✓ Liver function tests (Option 3): To detect hepatitis (rare) - check every 1-2 weeks during first 3 months ✓ Serum electrolytes including sodium (Option 5): To detect hyponatremia (common adverse effect) - check every 1-2 weeks during first 3 months ✓ The document states: "To improve detection of rare idiosyncratic reactions that usually occur in the first 3 months, complete blood count, electrolytes and liver function tests are suggested every 1-2 weeks during that time." vignette: A patient with chronic neuropathic pain is being considered for long-term opioid therapy. According to guidelines for use of opioids in chronic nonmalignant pain, which of the following are relative contraindications to opioid therapy?

Relative contraindications explicitly stated:

History of substance abuse (Option 2): Major contraindication due to addiction risk ✓ Frequent migraine headaches (Option 7): Listed as a relative contraindication ✓ Pain largely determined by psychological factors (Option 10): Listed as a relative contraindication ✓ Other relative contraindications mentioned:

vignette: Before prescribing tricyclic antidepressants for neuropathic pain, which of the following conditions are contraindications or require extreme caution?
stem: Select 3 or select "None" if none apply.

Pain relief (0-10 scale) (Option 2): Essential to assess efficacy ✓ Mood (Option 4): Important to monitor for depression and psychological well- being ✓ Side effects (Option 6): Must monitor for adverse effects Quality of life (Option 8): Important outcome measure Adherence to functional goals (Option 10): Critical to ensure opioids are improving function ✓ Presence of drug-related behavior (Option 12): Important for detecting misuse/addiction The document states: "The patient should be seen monthly or more often for the first few months and every 2-3 months thereafter. explanation: When medication is required, the safest effective agent should be used at the lowest dose for the shortest duration, with close follow-up.

stem: Which statements regarding pharmacologic treatment of insomnia are correct? Select ONE.

options.text: Hypnotics should be combined with alcohol
Supplies should be unlimited to avoid rebound insomnia

explanation: Hypnotics should not be combined with alcohol, should be time-limited, and off- label sedatives are not preferred.

vignette: Psychoses Total points7/10 A 22-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his parents. Over the past 3 months he has become increasingly suspicious, believes his neighbours are spying on him, and has been hearing voices telling him he is in danger. He has been socially withdrawn and stopped attending university. He has no prior psychiatric history. Urine drug screen is negative. His MRI brain is unremarkable. He is alert and cooperative. He is diagnosed with a first episode of psychosis.
stem: Which one of the following is the most appropriate initial pharmacologic treatment for this patient? Select 1.
explanation: Olanzapine 5 mg daily, titrating gradually ✓ — SGAs (excluding clozapine) are first- line for first-episode psychosis. Patients with first-episode psychosis are more responsive to lower doses, have a greater rate of recovery, and are more prone to side effects. The guideline is to start low and titrate gradually over 1–2 weeks.
Clozapine — Reserved exclusively for treatment-resistant schizophrenia due to risk of agranulocytosis and need for regular blood monitoring. Never first-line.
Haloperidol 20 mg daily — An FGA; high-potency agents carry greater EPS risk.
High doses are not more effective and are associated with more side effects. Even in chronic schizophrenia, 2–5 mg haloperidol is as effective as 10–40 mg.
Olanzapine 20 mg daily immediately — Excessively high starting dose; rapid titration and high doses do not accelerate response and increase adverse effects.
Maximum is usually 20 mg/day even in chronic illness.
Zuclopenthixol acetate injection — An injectable FGA explicitly contraindicated in antipsychotic-naïve first-episode patients.
None — Incorrect; a confirmed first episode of psychosis with functional impairment requires treatment.

vignette: The patient from Case 1 is started on olanzapine and achieves symptom remission and functional recovery.
stem: How long should maintenance antipsychotic therapy be continued? Select 1.
explanation: At least 1–2 years ✓ — For first-episode patients who achieve full symptom remission and functional recovery, maintenance pharmacotherapy should continue for at least 1–2 years per Canadian guidelines.
3 or 6 months — Far too short; first-episode psychosis carries a 70–90% risk of relapse within 5 years, and a significant percentage relapse as early as the second year after discontinuation.
At least 5 years — This applies to patients with 2 or more episodes, not to first- episode patients with full recovery.

Indefinitely in all cases — Indefinite treatment is recommended for many patients (particularly those with multiple episodes), but is not the universal standard for a first-episode patient who achieves full remission and recovery.

vignette: A 35-year-old woman with schizophrenia has been on risperidone for 2 years with good symptom control but has poor medication adherence due to forgetting her daily doses. She has relapsed twice.
stem: Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step? Select 1.

options.text: Add a second antipsychotic to ensure coverage
Increase risperidone to maximum oral dose

explanation: Risperidone LAI ✓ — The patient's relapses are due to nonadherence, not treatment failure. Long-acting injectable antipsychotics are specifically recommended to promote adherence, decrease relapse risk and hospitalization, and are appropriate in all phases of illness — especially in the first 2–5 years.
Patients who discontinue medications are 5 times more likely to relapse.

Add a second antipsychotic — Combination antipsychotic therapy is not supported by evidence and should only be used in exceptional circumstances under a psychiatrist. The issue here is adherence, not inadequate efficacy.
Increase risperidone oral dose — The problem is non-adherence, not underdosing.
Increasing the dose does not address missed doses.
Switch to clozapine — Reserved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia, not for adherence problems. This patient responds well to risperidone.
Switch to ziprasidone — No indication to switch agents when the current agent is effective; the clinical problem is adherence, not tolerability or efficacy.

vignette: A 45-year-old man with chronic schizophrenia on haloperidol develops repetitive involuntary lip-smacking and tongue movements.
stem: Which one of the following is the most appropriate management? Select 1.

options.text: Add benztropine to treat the movements
Add propranolol to treat the movements
Continue haloperidol and reassure the patient

explanation: Switch to an SGA ✓ — This patient has developed tardive dyskinesia (TD), characterized by repetitive involuntary choreoathetoid movements of the buccal- oral-lingual musculature. The incidence with FGAs is 5% per year. The recommended approach is to switch to an SGA, which carries a significantly lower risk of TD. For persistent severe TD, clozapine may be considered.
Add benztropine — Antiparkinsonian medications (anticholinergics) are not effective for TD and may actually worsen symptoms. They are useful for acute dystonia and parkinsonism, not TD.
Add propranolol — Propranolol (a beta-blocker) is the treatment of choice for akathisia, not TD.
Continue haloperidol and reassure — TD can be permanent and disabling; continuing the offending agent without action is inappropriate.
Increase the haloperidol dose — Increasing a high-potency FGA in a patient already developing TD would further worsen the condition.

vignette: A 28-year-old man with first-episode schizophrenia and a BMI of 30 is being started on an antipsychotic.
stem: Which one of the following SGAs is most appropriate given his metabolic risk profile? Select 1.
explanation: Lurasidone ✓ — In first-episode psychosis, treatment with an SGA with less risk of weight gain and metabolic side effects is recommended. Lurasidone is associated with minimal or no weight gain, and minimal risk of glucose abnormalities and dyslipidemia — making it ideal for a patient who is already overweight.
Clozapine — Associated with the greatest weight gain among all SGAs and highest risk of glucose abnormalities and hyperlipidemia. Also not first-line.
Olanzapine — Associated with the greatest weight gain among first-line SGAs, along with high risk of diabetes and dyslipidemia. Particularly inappropriate in a patient already with elevated BMI.
Quetiapine — Associated with moderate weight gain, increased triglycerides, and moderate metabolic risk. Not the best choice here.
Risperidone — Moderate weight gain and low but present metabolic risk.
Acceptable but not preferred over lurasidone in a high metabolic risk patient.

vignette: The patient in Case 1 is started on olanzapine.
stem: Which of the following are adverse effects of olanzapine that should be monitored and discussed with this patient? Select 3.

options.text: Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms (DRESS)
Weight gain and increased risk of diabetes

explanation: DRESS ✓ — Olanzapine is specifically associated with this rare but serious skin reaction with mortality rates up to 10%. It is listed explicitly in the drug table and requires patient counselling.
EPS, especially akathisia ✓ — Olanzapine can cause EPS, with akathisia being the most notable; listed in its adverse effects profile.
Weight gain and increased risk of diabetes ✓ — Olanzapine is among the highest- risk SGAs for weight gain and glucose abnormalities; essential counselling point especially in a young patient.
Agranulocytosis — This is the signature adverse effect of clozapine, not olanzapine.
Anticholinergic effects — While listed for olanzapine in the drug table, it is less prominent than weight gain, metabolic effects, and DRESS for counselling priority.
Bradycardia — Not a characteristic olanzapine adverse effect.
Hypoglycemia — Olanzapine causes hyperglycemia/diabetes, not hypoglycemia.
Significant hyperprolactinemia — Olanzapine causes only transient, minimal prolactin elevation; significant hyperprolactinemia is associated with risperidone, paliperidone, and high-potency FGAs.
Priapism — Associated with trazodone; not a characteristic olanzapine effect.

vignette: A patient with schizophrenia develops akathisia on their current antipsychotic. The dose has already been reduced and symptoms persist.
stem: Which of the following are appropriate management options? Select 2.
explanation: Propranolol ✓ — Beta-blockers (propranolol 10–120 mg/day) are explicitly the treatment of choice for akathisia when dose reduction is not effective, with monitoring for hypotension.
Lorazepam ✓ — Benzodiazepines are listed as providing symptom relief for akathisia.
Benztropine — Anticholinergics are explicitly stated to be ineffective for akathisia.
They are useful for acute dystonia and parkinsonism, not akathisia.
Increase the antipsychotic dose — Akathisia is often misidentified as psychotic agitation, but increasing the offending antipsychotic would worsen it; dose reduction is the first step, not increase.
Start clozapine immediately — Clozapine is reserved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia; not indicated for management of a side effect when other options exist.

vignette: A patient with schizophrenia is being considered for ziprasidone.
stem: Which of the following are important counselling or safety points specific to ziprasidone? Select 3.

options.text: Administer with a meal of at least 500 calories to maximize absorption
Can be freely combined with clarithromycin
Contraindicated in patients with a history of QTc prolongation
Dose changes can be made as frequently as every 3–4 days
Rapid titration is recommended to avoid ziprasidone-induced activation syndrome
Should be given once daily at bedtime

explanation: 500 calorie meal ✓ — Ziprasidone bioavailability is reduced by 50% if taken on an empty stomach; meals of at least 500 calories are required to maximize absorption and therapeutic serum concentrations.

Contraindicated with QTc prolongation history ✓ — Ziprasidone has a greater capacity for QTc prolongation compared with other antipsychotics and is contraindicated in patients with known QTc prolongation, congenital long QTc syndrome, recent MI, or uncompensated heart failure.

Rapid titration ✓ — Slow titration of ziprasidone is associated with poorer outcomes and development of activation syndrome (anxiety, restlessness, insomnia, increased energy) at lower doses (20–40 mg BID). Rapid titration to target dose is required.
Can be combined with clarithromycin — False; ziprasidone is contraindicated with any QTc-prolonging drug, explicitly including clarithromycin.
Dose changes every 3–4 days — This applies to aripiprazole (every 14 days due to long half-life). Ziprasidone requires rapid titration within the first week.
Once daily at bedtime — Ziprasidone requires twice-daily administration due to its short half-life of 6.6 hours.

stem: Regarding the use of long-acting injectable (LAI) antipsychotics in schizophrenia, which of the following statements are correct? Select 3.

options.text: LAIs are less effective than oral antipsychotics in controlling psychotic symptoms
LAIs are recommended especially in the first 2–5 years after illness onset
LAI usage rates in Canada are among the highest in the world
Paliperidone palmitate (Invega Sustenna) requires oral supplementation for the first 3 weeks after initiation
Risperidone LAI (Risperdal Consta) requires oral supplementation for the first 3 weeks after initiation
LAIs may improve remission rates and decrease risk of hospitalization and relapse

explanation: Recommended in first 2–5 years ✓ — LAIs are recommended in all phases but especially in the first 2–5 years after onset when patients are most vulnerable (the "critical period").

Risperidone LAI requires 3 weeks oral supplementation ✓ — Upon initiation of Risperdal Consta, oral supplementation with the current antipsychotic is required for the first 3 weeks because LAI risperidone takes time to reach therapeutic serum levels.
LAIs improve remission and reduce hospitalization ✓ — In addition to promoting adherence, LAIs may improve rates of remission and decrease the risk of hospitalization and relapse.
LAIs less effective than oral — False; LAIs are as effective as oral antipsychotics for controlling symptoms, with the added benefit of ensuring adherence.
Canada has among the highest LAI usage rates — False; LAI usage rates in Canada are low at 6.3%, compared with 15–80% in the rest of the world.

Paliperidone palmitate requires 3 weeks oral supplementation — False; this is a key distinguishing feature. Unlike risperidone LAI, paliperidone palmitate uses a loading dose strategy (2 initial injections 7 days apart) and does NOT require oral supplementation during initiation.

vignette: A 30-year-old woman with schizophrenia becomes pregnant.
stem: Which of the following are true regarding antipsychotic use during pregnancy? Select 3.

options.text: Antipsychotics are absolutely contraindicated in all trimesters of pregnancy
First-episode psychosis during pregnancy is a psychiatric emergency requiring treatment
Postpartum psychosis typically occurs within 2–4 weeks after delivery
Teratogenic effects including major congenital malformations have been clearly demonstrated with antipsychotic use
The risk of relapse in the postpartum period is high (~24%) and is greatest in the first 3 months
Use of antipsychotics during pregnancy has not been associated with an increased risk of gestational diabetes

explanation: Psychiatric emergency ✓ — The onset of a first episode of psychosis during pregnancy is considered a psychiatric emergency requiring treatment due to potential adverse effects on both mother and fetus, including doubled rates of stillbirth and infant death.

Postpartum psychosis within 2–4 weeks ✓ — The chapter explicitly states postpartum psychosis usually occurs within 2–4 weeks after delivery, at a rate of 1–2/1000 births, and is a psychiatric emergency due to rare but serious risk of suicide and infanticide.
~24% postpartum relapse risk in first 3 months ✓ — Explicitly stated: the risk of relapse of schizophrenia in the postpartum period is high (~24%) and is greatest during the first 3 months.

Absolutely contraindicated — False; for many women, maintenance antipsychotics during pregnancy at the lowest possible dose are recommended as maintenance therapy may reduce risks to the fetus associated with an acute psychotic relapse.

Major congenital malformations clearly demonstrated — False; the chapter explicitly states teratogenic effects including major congenital malformations have NOT been demonstrated with antipsychotic use.

Antipsychotics associated with gestational diabetes — False; the chapter explicitly states use of antipsychotics during pregnancy has NOT been associated with an increased risk of gestational diabetes.

vignette: A 32-year-old man presents requesting help to stop heroin use. He reports spending most of his day obtaining heroin, has tried unsuccessfully to quit multiple times, and continues using despite losing his job. Over the past 12 months, he has developed tolerance and withdrawal symptoms.
stem: How would you classify the severity of his opioid use disorder?
explanation: Severe opioid use disorder = ≥6 DSM-5 criteria within 12 months. He meets multiple criteria including tolerance and withdrawal .

vignette: A patient on chronic heroin use presents in moderate withdrawal. You plan to initiate buprenorphine/naloxone.
stem: Which of the following is required to avoid precipitated withdrawal?

options.label: A
options.text: Start immediately after last heroin use

options.label: B
options.text: Ensure patient is in moderate withdrawal

explanation: Buprenorphine may precipitate withdrawal if started too early because it is a partial agonist competing with full agonists. Start when moderate withdrawal is present (COWS ≥13)

stem: Which of the following is the standard of care for moderate to severe opioid use disorder?

options.label: C
options.text: Maintenance therapy with methadone or buprenorphine

options.label: E
options.text: Inpatient detox followed by discharge without maintenance

explanation: Maintenance therapy is superior to detoxification for relapse prevention, overdose reduction, and retention .

vignette: A patient on methadone maintenance therapy presents with syncope. ECG shows QTc prolongation.
stem: Which medication combination most increases this risk?
explanation: Methadone prolongs QTc and is contraindicated with high-risk QTc-prolonging agents such as citalopram

vignette: A 28-year-old pregnant woman with opioid use disorder asks about detoxification during pregnancy.
stem: What is the recommended approach?
explanation: Detoxification should be avoided in pregnancy due to risk of spontaneous abortion.
Maintenance therapy is standard of care.

vignette: A 34-year-old man with severe opioid use disorder presents requesting treatment. He injects heroin daily and has failed multiple detoxification attempts. He has no prolonged QT interval and no significant liver disease.
stem: Which of the following are appropriate first-line maintenance treatment options? Select ALL that apply.
explanation: Methadone and buprenorphine with naloxone are first-line maintenance treatments for moderate to severe opioid use disorder. Detoxification alone has high relapse risk.

vignette: A 29-year-old woman is found unresponsive with respiratory rate of 6 per minute and pinpoint pupils. Emergency medical services administer naloxone with improvement in respirations.
stem: Which of the following are appropriate management steps after initial reversal? Select ALL that apply.

options.text: Monitor for at least several hours
Consider repeat naloxone dosing if symptoms recur
Initiate methadone in the emergency department without assessment

explanation: Recurrent respiratory depression can occur due to shorter naloxone duration compared to many opioids. Monitoring, reassessment, and harm reduction counselling are required.

vignette: A 41-year-old man on methadone maintenance therapy presents with syncope. Electrocardiogram shows prolonged corrected QT interval.
stem: Which of the following factors increase the risk of methadone-related cardiac toxicity? Select ALL that apply.

options.text: Concomitant use of medications that prolong corrected QT interval

explanation: Methadone prolongs corrected QT interval. Risk increases with high doses, electrolyte abnormalities, interacting medications, structural heart disease, and bradycardia.

vignette: A 27-year-old pregnant woman with opioid use disorder asks about stopping all opioids immediately.
stem: Which of the following are appropriate management principles in pregnancy? Select ALL that apply.
explanation: Maintenance therapy is recommended in pregnancy. Abrupt detoxification increases risk of fetal loss and relapse. Multidisciplinary monitoring is essential.

vignette: A 38-year-old man in early opioid withdrawal presents with sweating, piloerection, abdominal cramps, and anxiety. He declines opioid agonist therapy.
stem: Which of the following medications may be used for symptomatic management? Select ALL that apply.
explanation: Clonidine reduces autonomic symptoms. Loperamide treats diarrhea. Ondansetron helps nausea. Analgesics may be used for pain. Benzodiazepine monotherapy is not appropriate treatment for opioid withdrawal.

Report Forms Smoking cessation Total points9/10 A 45-year-old man presents to his family physician requesting help to quit smoking. He smokes 25 cigarettes per day and has his first cigarette within 10 minutes of waking. He has tried quitting twice before using willpower alone and relapsed both times. He has no history of seizures, eating disorders, or psychiatric illness. He has no other medical conditions and takes no medications. He is highly motivated to quit and has set a quit date in 2 weeks.

stem: Which one of the following is the most appropriate first-line pharmacologic treatment for this patient? Select 1.

options.label: F
options.text: None — behavioural therapy only is sufficient

explanation: Varenicline — This patient smokes more than 10 cigarettes per day, is highly motivated, and has no contraindications. Among pharmacotherapies, varenicline has the highest odds ratio for cessation compared to nicotine patch and bupropion. It is an appropriate first-line choice for a highly dependent smoker.
Clonidine — A second-line agent without an official indication for smoking cessation; reserved for those with coexisting hypertension or when first-line therapies have failed.

Cytisine — Available in Canada without a prescription and has efficacy over placebo, but its role is still under review and it is not established as a preferred first-line agent over varenicline for a highly dependent smoker.
Nortriptyline — A second-line agent used when first-line therapies are unaffordable or unsuccessful; caution required in cardiovascular disease.

Nicotine patch monotherapy — Appropriate first-line for many patients, but combination NRT or varenicline is preferred in a highly dependent smoker (25 cigarettes/day, first cigarette within 10 minutes of waking = high dependence).

Behavioural therapy only — Pharmacotherapy is recommended for all patients who smoke more than 10 cigarettes/day and wish to quit; combining pharmacotherapy with behavioural support is better than either alone.

vignette: The patient from Case 1 is started on varenicline.
stem: Which one of the following is the most appropriate instruction regarding when to set the quit date relative to starting varenicline? Select 1.

options.label: A
options.text: Quit smoking on the same day varenicline is started

options.label: B
options.text: Quit smoking 1–2 weeks after starting varenicline

options.label: C
options.text: Quit smoking 4–6 weeks after starting varenicline

options.label: D
options.text: Varenicline must be started on the quit date itself

options.label: E
options.text: There is no relationship between varenicline start date and quit date

explanation: Quit smoking 1–2 weeks after starting — The product guideline for varenicline states the patient should quit smoking 1–2 weeks after starting the medication, allowing time for the drug to reach steady state and begin partial agonist effects at nicotinic receptors.
Same day — Incorrect; varenicline needs time to reach effective levels before the quit attempt.
4–6 weeks after — Too long; if the patient is still smoking 4 weeks after starting, therapy should be reassessed.
Must start on quit date — This applies to the nicotine patch (started on the quit date), not varenicline.
No relationship — False; timing of varenicline initiation relative to the quit date is specifically addressed in guidelines.

vignette: A 38-year-old woman who smokes 30 cigarettes per day has a history of a generalized tonic-clonic seizure 3 years ago following a head injury. She has been seizure-free since and takes no anticonvulsants. She wants help quitting smoking.
stem: Which one of the following medications is contraindicated in this patient? Select 1.
explanation: Bupropion — Explicitly contraindicated in patients with a history of seizures or conditions predisposing to seizures. This patient has a documented prior seizure, making bupropion contraindicated regardless of current seizure-free status.
Clonidine — No seizure-related contraindication; main concerns are hypotension and rebound hypertension.
Nicotine transdermal patch — No contraindication in seizure history; a safe first- line option.
Nortriptyline — No absolute contraindication in seizure history; caution mainly in cardiovascular disease.
Varenicline — No contraindication in seizure history; neuropsychiatric monitoring is required.

vignette: A patient with schizophrenia who is stable on olanzapine successfully quits smoking with varenicline.
stem: Which one of the following medication adjustments is most likely required after smoking cessation? Select 1.

options.label: A
options.text: Decrease olanzapine dose due to reduced CYP1A2 induction

options.label: B
options.text: Increase olanzapine dose due to reduced absorption

options.label: C
options.text: No change to olanzapine is needed

options.label: D
options.text: Switch olanzapine to a different antipsychotic

explanation: Decrease olanzapine — Cigarette smoke contains polyaromatic hydrocarbons that induce CYP1A2, increasing the clearance of olanzapine. Smokers require higher doses. When a patient quits smoking, CYP1A2 induction is lost, clearance decreases, and olanzapine levels rise — requiring dose reduction to avoid toxicity.
Increase dose — Incorrect; quitting smoking increases drug levels.
No change — Incorrect; this is a well-documented pharmacokinetic interaction.
Switch medication — Not indicated; the issue is metabolic, not drug failure.
Stop varenicline — Incorrect; varenicline should be continued for 12 weeks (and may be extended).

vignette: A pregnant woman at 14 weeks gestation smokes 20 cigarettes per day. She has tried behavioural strategies alone but cannot stop.
stem: Which one of the following is the most appropriate pharmacologic approach? Select 1.

options.label: B
options.text: Nicotine polacrilex gum (short-acting NRT) at the lowest effective dose

options.label: C
options.text: Nicotine transdermal patch 21 mg worn continuously for 24 hours

explanation: Nicotine polacrilex gum — In pregnant women unable to quit using behavioural measures alone, the guideline recommends the lowest effective dose of short- acting nicotine to eliminate smoke exposure while minimizing fetal nicotine exposure.
Bupropion — May be used especially with comorbid depression, but not first choice when NRT can be attempted.
Patch 21 mg continuous — Patch reserved for heavy dependence if gum fails and should be removed after 16 hours, not worn 24 hours.
Nortriptyline — Second-line agent; not appropriate in pregnancy without clear indication.
Varenicline — Safety data in pregnancy remain limited; not recommended.

vignette: The patient in Case 1 is started on varenicline.
stem: Which of the following are adverse effects of varenicline that should be discussed with him before starting? Select 3.

options.text: Potential neuropsychiatric effects including mood changes and suicidal/homicidal ideation

explanation: Nausea — Occurs in approximately 30% of patients; may be reduced by taking with food and water.
Insomnia — Common; second dose should be taken at suppertime.
Neuropsychiatric effects — Boxed warning includes potential mood and behavioural changes.
Other options correspond to adverse effects of other drug classes.

stem: Regarding the use of nicotine replacement therapy (NRT), which of the following statements are correct? Select 3.

options.text: Combining patch with as-needed gum or inhaler is more effective than single products
Extending NRT beyond 24 weeks provides significant additional benefit
NRT is contraindicated in patients who smoke more than 20 cigarettes/day
Patches should be started 1–2 weeks before quit date
Standard duration is 8–12 weeks; extending to 24 weeks can improve rates

explanation: Combination NRT — More effective due to steady baseline plus breakthrough dosing.
50–70% improvement — Established efficacy benchmark.
8–12 weeks standard — Extension to 24 weeks improves rates; beyond 24 weeks shows no additional benefit.

vignette: A patient on clonidine for smoking cessation is being counselled about its use.
stem: Which of the following are important safety and counselling points specific to clonidine? Select 3.

options.text: Avoid concurrent use with tricyclic antidepressants
Monitor blood pressure and heart rate
Must be tapered to avoid rebound hypertension
Sedation, dizziness, hypotension, dry mouth common

explanation: (If restricted to 3: prioritize 4, 5, 6)
Clonidine must be tapered to avoid rebound hypertension.
Blood pressure and heart rate must be monitored.
Common adverse effects include sedation, dizziness, hypotension, and dry mouth.
Concurrent TCA use should be avoided due to interaction.

vignette: When a patient who smokes quits smoking, dose reductions may be required for certain medications due to changes in CYP1A2 activity.
stem: Which of the following medications may require dose reduction after smoking cessation? Select 3.
explanation: (If restricted to 3: prioritize 3, 5, 7)
Smoking induces CYP1A2. When smoking stops, levels of clozapine, olanzapine, and theophylline rise and require dose reduction.
Caffeine metabolism also slows, increasing side effects.

stem: Regarding pharmacotherapy for smoking cessation in pregnancy, which of the following statements are correct? Select 3.

options.text: Bupropion use during pregnancy has not been associated with a higher risk of congenital malformations
Data on varenicline safety in pregnancy are sufficient to recommend it routinely
If NRT is used in pregnancy, the transdermal patch should be removed at bedtime to reduce fetal nicotine exposure
NRT carries no risks whatsoever during pregnancy
Pharmacotherapy should be avoided unless the woman is unable to quit using behavioural measures alone
The risks of continued smoking always outweigh any risks of pharmacotherapy in pregnancy

explanation: Bupropion has not been linked to a higher rate of congenital malformations, so it may be considered when behavioural measures fail.
Varenicline safety data in pregnancy remain insufficient for routine recommendation.
If NRT is used, removing the patch at bedtime limits fetal nicotine exposure.
NRT is not risk-free, and pharmacotherapy is reserved for women unable to quit with behavioural support alone.

vignette: A 9-year-old boy is diagnosed with combined inattentive and hyperactive symptoms. He has no cardiac history. His parents prefer once-daily dosing because he forgets afternoon doses at school.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line pharmacologic option?
explanation: Explanation Long-acting stimulant formulations are recommended first-line because they:
Provide 8–14 hours of coverage Improve adherence Avoid in-school dosing Reduce rebound symptoms Lower diversion risk Immediate-release formulations require multiple daily dosing.
Clonidine is second- or third-line and primarily improves hyperactivity and impulsivity.
Bupropion is second-line and less effective than stimulants.
Risperidone does not treat core inattentive symptoms and is reserved for severe behavioural issues.

vignette: A 15-year-old girl with attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder develops persistent insomnia, appetite suppression, and has lost 12 percent of her baseline weight over three months on lisdexamfetamine. Her academic performance has improved significantly.
stem: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: D
options.text: Consider a brief drug holiday or dose adjustment

explanation: Explanation Weight loss greater than 10 percent and growth concerns warrant reassessment.
Appropriate strategies include:
Dose reduction Brief drug holiday during low academic demand Careful growth monitoring Permanent discontinuation is not required if benefits outweigh risks.
Adding risperidone does not address appetite suppression.
Continuing unchanged despite significant weight loss is inappropriate.

vignette: A 12-year-old boy with attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder has a strong family history of sudden cardiac death. His physical examination reveals elevated resting heart rate.
stem: Which of the following is most appropriate before starting stimulant therapy?

options.label: C
options.text: Start stimulant at half-dose without evaluation

options.label: E
options.text: Refer directly for behavioural therapy only

explanation: Explanation Routine electrocardiogram is not required for all patients.
However, it is reasonable when:
Personal or family history of cardiac disease Elevated blood pressure or heart rate History of sudden cardiac death This patient meets those criteria.
Starting stimulant without evaluation is inappropriate.
Atomoxetine also carries cardiovascular warnings.

vignette: A 17-year-old adolescent with attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder and comorbid substance use disorder requires treatment.
stem: Which medication is most appropriate?
explanation: Explanation Atomoxetine:
Is not a controlled substance Has no abuse potential Is recommended in patients with substance use disorder Improves core symptoms over 6–12 weeks Stimulants carry diversion and misuse risk.

vignette: An 8-year-old child with attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder has persistent severe impulsivity and aggression despite adequate stimulant trial. There is comorbid oppositional defiant disorder.
stem: What is the most appropriate next pharmacologic strategy?

options.label: E
options.text: Discontinue stimulants and use risperidone monotherapy

explanation: Explanation Guanfacine:

Targets impulsivity and aggression Useful in comorbid oppositional defiant disorder Can be used adjunctively with stimulants Has less sedation and hypotension than clonidine Risperidone may be used in severe behavioural dysregulation but does not improve inattention and carries metabolic risk.
Venlafaxine and imipramine are not first add-on options.

vignette: A 10-year-old boy with attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder is starting stimulant therapy. His parents ask about common adverse effects.
stem: Which of the following are recognized adverse effects of stimulant medications?
explanation: Stimulants commonly cause appetite suppression, insomnia, mild increases in heart rate and blood pressure, and irritability. Long-term therapy may affect growth velocity. Neutropenia and blindness are not typical adverse effects.

vignette: A 14-year-old girl is being considered for atomoxetine after poor tolerance of stimulant therapy.
stem: Which statements about atomoxetine are accurate?

options.text: It is a selective norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor
It may take several weeks to show benefit
It carries warning regarding suicidal ideation

explanation: Atomoxetine is a selective norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor. It is not a controlled substance. Clinical response may take several weeks. It carries a warning regarding suicidal ideation and may increase blood pressure.

vignette: A 7-year-old child with attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder has difficulty falling asleep after evening stimulant dosing.
stem: Which management strategies are appropriate?

options.text: Move stimulant dose earlier in the day
Reduce stimulant dose if clinically appropriate

explanation: Insomnia can be managed by adjusting timing, reducing dose, switching formulation, or considering melatonin. Evening caffeine or increasing stimulant dose at bedtime would worsen symptoms.

vignette: A 16-year-old boy with attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder reports mood instability and periods of decreased need for sleep. Family history reveals bipolar disorder.
stem: Which actions are appropriate before initiating stimulant therapy?

options.text: Initiate stimulant immediately regardless of mood symptoms
Begin high-dose stimulant to clarify diagnosis

explanation: Stimulants may exacerbate bipolar disorder. Screening and stabilization of mood disorder are essential before starting stimulant therapy. Psychiatric referral may be warranted.

vignette: A 27-year-old pregnant woman with active bulimia nervosa presents for prenatal care.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate management principle?

options.label: B
options.text: Ignore purging behavior if fetal growth is normal

options.label: C
options.text: Prioritize nonpharmacologic therapy when possible and assess maternal risk

options.label: E
options.text: Begin stimulant medication for appetite control

explanation: In pregnancy, individualized risk-benefit assessment is required.
Nonpharmacologic therapy is preferred when possible, but maternal safety and psychiatric stability must be prioritized.

vignette: A 29-year-old woman presents with excessive worry occurring most days for over eight months. She reports difficulty controlling the worry, muscle tension, irritability, and poor sleep. There are no panic attacks.
stem: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacologic treatment?
explanation: This presentation is consistent with generalized anxiety disorder. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors such as sertraline are first-line treatment.
Benzodiazepines are not first-line long-term therapy. Antipsychotics are not first- line for uncomplicated anxiety.

vignette: A 34-year-old man presents with sudden episodes of intense fear, palpitations, sweating, and shortness of breath lasting 15 minutes. He now avoids public spaces for fear of another episode.
stem: Which features support a diagnosis of panic disorder with agoraphobia?

options.text: Avoidance of situations due to fear of escape difficulty
Fear limited to social scrutiny only
At least one month of behavioral change

explanation: Panic disorder requires recurrent unexpected attacks plus persistent concern or maladaptive behaviour change for at least one month. Avoidance due to fear of being unable to escape supports agoraphobia. Substance-induced or medical causes must be excluded.

vignette: A 41-year-old woman with generalized anxiety disorder has been on sertraline for three weeks with partial improvement. She reports persistent insomnia and muscle tension.
stem: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: F
options.text: Stop all pharmacotherapy and use only herbal remedies

explanation: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors require adequate dose titration and sufficient duration before determining nonresponse. Three weeks is often too early to declare treatment failure.

vignette: A 27-year-old pregnant woman at 20 weeks gestation presents with severe generalized anxiety disorder impairing function. Nonpharmacologic therapy has not been sufficient.
stem: Which principles apply to management?

options.text: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors may be considered when benefits outweigh risks
Informed consent regarding risks is required
Benzodiazepines are risk free in pregnancy

explanation: Nonpharmacologic treatment is first-line. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors may be used when clinically necessary. Absolute contraindication is incorrect. Risks must be discussed.

vignette: A 22-year-old university student presents with marked fear of public speaking. She experiences blushing, tremor, and intense fear during presentations but is otherwise functional.
stem: Most appropriate first-line treatment for performance-only social anxiety?
explanation: Beta-adrenergic antagonists such as propranolol may be used for performance- only social anxiety to reduce autonomic symptoms.

vignette: A 45-year-old man with generalized anxiety disorder is started on escitalopram.
stem: Which counseling points are appropriate?

options.text: Initial increase in anxiety may occur
Therapeutic effect may take several weeks
Abrupt discontinuation may cause withdrawal symptoms
Alcohol should be avoided or minimized

explanation: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors may initially worsen anxiety and require weeks for effect. Gradual discontinuation is necessary. Alcohol may worsen symptoms.

vignette: A 36-year-old woman with panic disorder is requesting long-term benzodiazepine therapy because it provides rapid relief.
stem: Which concerns are valid regarding chronic benzodiazepine use?

options.text: Risk of falls in older adults
Increased mortality in combination with opioids

explanation: Benzodiazepines carry risks of dependence, cognitive effects, withdrawal, and increased mortality when combined with opioids.

vignette: A 30-year-old woman presents with obsessive intrusive thoughts about contamination and repetitive handwashing. Symptoms consume more than two hours daily.
stem: Which treatments are evidence-based?
explanation: Obsessive-compulsive disorder responds to selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors and exposure-based cognitive behavioural therapy. Antipsychotic augmentation may be used in refractory cases.

vignette: A 50-year-old man presents with chronic excessive health-related worry despite normal investigations. He repeatedly seeks reassurance.
stem: Most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Illness anxiety disorder involves persistent preoccupation with having a serious illness despite reassurance and minimal somatic symptoms.

vignette: A 60-year-old patient with anxiety disorder is being evaluated before starting pharmacotherapy.
stem: Which baseline assessments are appropriate?

options.text: Thyroid function testing if clinically indicated

explanation: Assessment should include substance use, bipolar screening, suicidality, medical causes when indicated, and medication interactions. Routine electroencephalogram is not required.

vignette: A 64-year-old man presents to the emergency department with 45 minutes of central chest pressure radiating to his left arm. He is diaphoretic and nauseated. Blood pressure is 138/82 mmHg, heart rate 92 beats per minute. An electrocardiogram shows ST-segment elevation in leads II, III, and aVF.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.label: E
options.text: Observe and repeat electrocardiogram in 30 minutes

explanation: This patient has an ST-elevation myocardial infarction. Immediate reperfusion therapy is the priority and should not be delayed by additional testing or non- definitive treatments.

vignette: Before reperfusion therapy is initiated, which interventions should be performed immediately?
stem: Select 5.

options.text: Obtain informed consent for thrombolysis only
Place the patient on continuous cardiac monitoring
Delay treatment until cardiac biomarkers return

explanation: Immediate management includes antiplatelet therapy, monitoring, intravenous access, pain control, and assessment for reperfusion contraindications. Routine oxygen and delays for biomarkers are inappropriate.

vignette: A 71-year-old woman presents with chest discomfort and shortness of breath. Her electrocardiogram shows ST-segment depression in the lateral leads. Initial troponin is elevated.
stem: Which diagnosis best explains this presentation?
explanation: ST-segment depression with positive cardiac biomarkers indicates myocardial necrosis without ST elevation, consistent with non–ST-elevation myocardial infarction.

sharedCase: A 71-year-old woman presents with chest discomfort and shortness of breath. Her electrocardiogram shows ST-segment depression in the lateral leads. Initial troponin is elevated.
stem: Which factors increase this patient's short-term risk and support an early invasive strategy? Select 4.
explanation: Ongoing ischemia, electrocardiographic changes, older age, and instability identify high-risk patients who benefit from early invasive management.

vignette: A 59-year-old man with acute coronary syndrome is started on dual antiplatelet therapy and anticoagulation. He has a history of peptic ulcer disease with recent gastrointestinal bleeding.
stem: Which anticoagulation strategy is most appropriate?

options.label: C
options.text: Anticoagulation with careful bleeding risk assessment

explanation: Patients with high bleeding risk still require antithrombotic therapy, but selection and dosing must balance ischemic benefit and bleeding risk.

sharedCase: A 59-year-old man with acute coronary syndrome is started on dual antiplatelet therapy and anticoagulation. He has a history of peptic ulcer disease with recent gastrointestinal bleeding.
stem: Which factors increase bleeding risk in patients with acute coronary syndrome receiving antithrombotic therapy? Select 6.
explanation: Age, prior bleeding, renal dysfunction, low body weight, stroke history, and female sex are recognized bleeding risk factors in acute coronary syndrome management.

vignette: A 66-year-old man with non–ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome is clinically stable after initial management.
stem: Which medication should be initiated early to reduce long-term mortality?
explanation: High-intensity statin therapy reduces recurrent ischemic events and mortality and should be initiated early in acute coronary syndrome.

sharedCase: A 66-year-old man with non–ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome is clinically stable after initial management.
stem: Which effects should be discussed with the patient when initiating high-intensity statin therapy? Select 4.
explanation: Patients should be counselled on common and clinically relevant statin effects, including muscle symptoms, liver enzyme changes, gastrointestinal effects, and cardiovascular benefit.

vignette: A 58-year-old man with ST-elevation myocardial infarction undergoes successful percutaneous coronary intervention. He is hemodynamically stable.
stem: Which beta-blocker strategy is most appropriate?

options.label: D
options.text: Start beta-blocker only if hypertension develops

explanation: Oral beta-blockers should be initiated once the patient is stable to reduce reinfarction and arrhythmia risk. Routine early intravenous dosing increases the risk of shock.

sharedCase: A 58-year-old man with ST-elevation myocardial infarction undergoes successful percutaneous coronary intervention. He is hemodynamically stable.
stem: Which conditions are contraindications to early beta-blocker use in acute coronary syndrome? Select 5.
explanation: Beta-blockers should be avoided in patients with instability, conduction abnormalities, bronchospasm, or shock due to risk of clinical deterioration.

vignette: Prevention of Ischemic stroke Total points8/10 A 67-year-old man presents with a transient episode of right arm weakness and expressive aphasia lasting 15 minutes, which resolved completely. This occurred 24 hours ago. He has hypertension and type 2 diabetes.
stem: Which investigation should be performed urgently?

options.label: C
options.text: CT scan of the brain with vascular imaging

explanation: Patients with recent transient ischemic attack require urgent brain imaging to exclude hemorrhage or mimics and to assess vascular anatomy. CT with angiography is appropriate as an initial investigation.

sharedCase: Prevention of Ischemic stroke Total points8/10 A 67-year-old man presents with a transient episode of right arm weakness and expressive aphasia lasting 15 minutes, which resolved completely. This occurred 24 hours ago. He has hypertension and type 2 diabetes.
stem: Which features increase the short-term risk of stroke after a transient ischemic attack? Select ALL that apply.

options.text: Symptoms occurring more than one month ago

explanation: Older age, diabetes, prolonged symptoms, and motor or speech deficits are associated with a higher early stroke risk after transient ischemic attack.

vignette: A 72-year-old woman with a recent noncardioembolic ischemic stroke is being started on long-term antithrombotic therapy. She has no history of atrial fibrillation.
stem: Which medication is most appropriate?
explanation: Antiplatelet therapy is the treatment of choice for secondary prevention of noncardioembolic ischemic stroke. Oral anticoagulants are reserved for cardioembolic sources.

stem: Which antithrombotic strategies are appropriate for long-term secondary prevention after noncardioembolic ischemic stroke? Select ONE.
explanation: Single-agent antiplatelet therapy is recommended for long-term secondary prevention. Anticoagulation and prolonged dual antiplatelet therapy are not indicated in this setting.

vignette: A 65-year-old man experiences a recurrent transient ischemic attack while taking acetylsalicylic acid 81 mg daily. He is adherent to therapy.
stem: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: B
options.text: Add long-term clopidogrel to acetylsalicylic acid

explanation: In patients with recurrent ischemic events while taking acetylsalicylic acid, switching to an alternative antiplatelet agent such as clopidogrel is reasonable.

sharedCase: A 65-year-old man experiences a recurrent transient ischemic attack while taking acetylsalicylic acid 81 mg daily. He is adherent to therapy.
stem: Which antiplatelet regimens are NOT recommended for long-term secondary stroke prevention? Select ALL that apply.
explanation: Long-term dual antiplatelet therapy increases bleeding risk without additional benefit, and anticoagulation is not indicated in the absence of a cardioembolic source.

vignette: A 69-year-old woman has symptomatic carotid artery stenosis of 75% confirmed on imaging following a transient ischemic attack.
stem: What is the most appropriate management?

options.label: B
options.text: Carotid artery stenting in all cases

explanation: Patients with symptomatic high-grade carotid stenosis benefit from carotid endarterectomy performed within two weeks of the ischemic event when surgical risk is acceptable.

sharedCase: A 69-year-old woman has symptomatic carotid artery stenosis of 75% confirmed on imaging following a transient ischemic attack.
stem: Which findings support carotid endarterectomy rather than medical management alone? Select ALL that apply.

options.text: Life expectancy less than one year

explanation: Endarterectomy is beneficial in patients with symptomatic high-grade stenosis when operative risk is low and symptoms correspond to the affected artery.

vignette: A 58-year-old woman with a history of ischemic stroke asks about restarting combined oral contraceptives.
stem: What is the most appropriate advice?
explanation: Combined oral contraceptives increase the risk of ischemic stroke and should be avoided in patients with a history of stroke or transient ischemic attack.

stem: Which statements regarding hormonal therapy and stroke prevention are correct? Select NONE.

options.text: Estrogen therapy reduces recurrent stroke risk
Combined estrogen–progestin therapy is protective after stroke
Hormonal therapy is recommended after transient ischemic attack
Hormonal therapy lowers cardiovascular mortality after stroke

explanation: Hormonal therapy does not provide protection against recurrent stroke and may increase vascular risk; therefore, none of the listed statements are correct.

vignette: Primary Prevention of vascular disease Total points7/10 A 52-year-old man with no history of cardiovascular disease presents for a routine visit. He is overweight, sedentary, and has a blood pressure of 138/86 mmHg. He does not smoke and has no diabetes.
stem: What is the most appropriate initial intervention to reduce his vascular risk?
explanation: Lifestyle modification is the foundation of primary prevention and should be initiated early in patients without established vascular disease.

sharedCase: Primary Prevention of vascular disease Total points7/10 A 52-year-old man with no history of cardiovascular disease presents for a routine visit. He is overweight, sedentary, and has a blood pressure of 138/86 mmHg. He does not smoke and has no diabetes.
stem: Which interventions are components of lifestyle modification shown to reduce vascular risk? Select ONE.
explanation: Regular moderate-intensity physical activity reduces vascular risk. Antioxidant and vitamin supplementation have not demonstrated benefit.

vignette: A 60-year-old woman with hypertension and dyslipidemia has no history of myocardial infarction or stroke. Her calculated 10-year cardiovascular risk is low.
stem: Which statement best describes the role of statin therapy in this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Statins are mandatory regardless of risk

options.label: C
options.text: Statins may be considered based on overall risk and patient preference

options.label: D
options.text: Statins provide large absolute risk reduction in low-risk patients

options.label: E
options.text: Statins replace the need for lifestyle modification

explanation: In primary prevention, statins may be considered based on overall risk and shared decision-making, with modest absolute benefit in low-risk patients.

sharedCase: A 60-year-old woman with hypertension and dyslipidemia has no history of myocardial infarction or stroke. Her calculated 10-year cardiovascular risk is low.
stem: Which statements regarding statin therapy in primary prevention are correct? Select ALL that apply.

options.text: Statins replace the need for lifestyle modification
Absolute risk reduction is smaller than in secondary prevention
Most benefit is seen in very low-risk individuals
Relative risk reduction is similar to secondary prevention

explanation: Statins lower low-density lipoprotein cholesterol and offer similar relative risk reduction to secondary prevention, but the absolute benefit is smaller in primary prevention.

vignette: A 64-year-old man with no prior vascular events asks about taking acetylsalicylic acid to prevent myocardial infarction. He has controlled hypertension and no history of gastrointestinal bleeding.
stem: Which statement best reflects current evidence?

options.label: A
options.text: Acetylsalicylic acid is recommended for all adults over 60

options.label: B
options.text: Acetylsalicylic acid provides substantial net benefit in primary prevention

options.label: C
options.text: Acetylsalicylic acid may be considered if cardiovascular benefit outweighs bleeding risk

options.label: D
options.text: Acetylsalicylic acid has no bleeding risk

options.label: E
options.text: Acetylsalicylic acid prevents stroke more than myocardial infarction

explanation: In primary prevention, benefits are modest and must be weighed against bleeding risk; use is individualized.

sharedCase: A 64-year-old man with no prior vascular events asks about taking acetylsalicylic acid to prevent myocardial infarction. He has controlled hypertension and no history of gastrointestinal bleeding.
stem: Which factors increase the risk of bleeding with acetylsalicylic acid use? Select ALL that apply.
explanation: Bleeding risk increases with older age, peptic ulcer disease, concurrent nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug use, and anticoagulation.

vignette: A 55-year-old woman who smokes asks about smoking cessation aids to reduce her vascular risk.
stem: Which intervention has evidence supporting improved quit rates?
explanation: Nicotine replacement therapy improves quit rates and reduces vascular risk.
Vitamin and omega-3 supplementation are not smoking cessation treatments.

sharedCase: A 55-year-old woman who smokes asks about smoking cessation aids to reduce her vascular risk.
stem: Which smoking cessation strategies are supported by evidence? Select ALL that apply.
explanation: Behavioural counselling and pharmacotherapy (nicotine replacement therapy, varenicline, bupropion) improve quit rates.

vignette: A 70-year-old woman asks whether vitamin D and multivitamins reduce her risk of stroke or myocardial infarction.
stem: What is the most appropriate response?

options.label: B
options.text: Recommend vitamin D supplementation for vascular protection

options.label: D
options.text: Advise that supplements have not demonstrated vascular risk reduction

explanation: Nutritional supplements have not consistently demonstrated reduction in vascular events in primary prevention.

stem: Which nutritional supplements have demonstrated proven benefit in primary prevention of vascular disease? Select NONE.
explanation: No listed supplements have consistently demonstrated proven vascular risk reduction in primary prevention.

vignette: Supraventricular Tachycardia Total points6/10 A 28-year-old woman presents with sudden-onset palpitations and lightheadedness. Her heart rate is 180 beats per minute, regular, with narrow QRS complexes. Blood pressure is stable.
stem: What is the most appropriate initial management?
explanation: In a hemodynamically stable patient with narrow-complex tachycardia, vagal manoeuvres are the recommended first intervention.

sharedCase: Supraventricular Tachycardia Total points6/10 A 28-year-old woman presents with sudden-onset palpitations and lightheadedness. Her heart rate is 180 beats per minute, regular, with narrow QRS complexes. Blood pressure is stable.
stem: Which features are consistent with supraventricular tachycardia rather than ventricular tachycardia? Select ALL that apply
explanation: Supraventricular tachycardia typically presents with narrow complexes, sudden onset and termination, and may respond to vagal manoeuvres. AV dissociation suggests ventricular tachycardia.

vignette: A 35-year-old man with recurrent episodes of supraventricular tachycardia presents to the emergency department. Vagal manoeuvres are unsuccessful. He remains stable.
stem: Which medication is most appropriate next?
explanation: Intravenous adenosine is the drug of choice for acute termination of stable supraventricular tachycardia when vagal manoeuvres fail.

sharedCase: A 35-year-old man with recurrent episodes of supraventricular tachycardia presents to the emergency department. Vagal manoeuvres are unsuccessful. He remains stable.
stem: Which conditions are contraindications to adenosine use? Select ONE
explanation: Adenosine can provoke bronchospasm and should be avoided in patients with active asthma.

vignette: A 42-year-old woman with supraventricular tachycardia becomes hypotensive and confused during an episode.
stem: What is the most appropriate immediate intervention?
explanation: Hemodynamic instability in supraventricular tachycardia requires immediate synchronized cardioversion.

sharedCase: A 42-year-old woman with supraventricular tachycardia becomes hypotensive and confused during an episode.
stem: Which findings indicate hemodynamic instability during supraventricular tachycardia? Select ALL that apply.
explanation: Hypotension, chest pain, and altered mental status indicate compromised perfusion and require urgent intervention.

vignette: A 30-year-old man has frequent episodes of paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia despite medical therapy and prefers definitive treatment.
stem: Which intervention offers the highest likelihood of cure?
explanation: Catheter ablation targets the arrhythmogenic pathway and offers a high cure rate for most supraventricular tachycardias.

sharedCase: A 30-year-old man has frequent episodes of paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia despite medical therapy and prefers definitive treatment.
stem: Which patients are appropriate candidates for catheter ablation in supraventricular tachycardia? Select ALL that apply
explanation: Ablation is appropriate for patients with recurrent symptoms, medication intolerance or failure, and those desiring definitive treatment.

vignette: A patient with supraventricular tachycardia is found to have atrioventricular nodal re-entry tachycardia.
stem: Which statement best describes this arrhythmia?

options.label: C
options.text: It involves dual pathways within the atrioventricular node

options.label: D
options.text: It is always associated with structural heart disease

explanation: Atrioventricular nodal re-entry tachycardia results from re-entry involving dual conduction pathways within the atrioventricular node.

stem: Which statements regarding atrioventricular nodal re-entry tachycardia are correct? Select NONE

options.text: It is the most common form of supraventricular tachycardia
It typically presents with sudden onset palpitations

explanation: Atrioventricular nodal re-entry tachycardia does not require anticoagulation, and the other statements are true.

vignette: A 68-year-old man presents after a brief loss of consciousness while standing in a grocery store line. He recovered within seconds and has no post-event confusion. He reports lightheadedness and nausea beforehand. Examination and electrocardiogram are normal.
stem: What is the most likely cause of his episode?
explanation: Prodromal symptoms such as nausea and lightheadedness, rapid recovery, and normal examination are typical of vasovagal syncope.

sharedCase: A 68-year-old man presents after a brief loss of consciousness while standing in a grocery store line. He recovered within seconds and has no post-event confusion. He reports lightheadedness and nausea beforehand. Examination and electrocardiogram are normal.
stem: Which features support vasovagal syncope rather than cardiac syncope? Select ALL that apply.

options.text: Presence of diaphoresis before the event

explanation: Vasovagal syncope is associated with autonomic prodromal symptoms, prolonged standing, and rapid recovery without neurologic deficit.

vignette: A 74-year-old woman experiences recurrent syncope when turning her head or shaving her neck. Cardiac evaluation is otherwise unremarkable.
stem: What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Syncope triggered by neck movement or pressure is characteristic of carotid sinus hypersensitivity, particularly in older adults.

sharedCase: A 74-year-old woman experiences recurrent syncope when turning her head or shaving her neck. Cardiac evaluation is otherwise unremarkable.
stem: Which investigations are appropriate in the initial evaluation of syncope in adults? Select ALL that apply.
explanation: Initial evaluation includes electrocardiography, review of medications that may contribute to syncope, and assessment for orthostatic hypotension. Routine neuroimaging is not indicated.

vignette: A 63-year-old man with a history of myocardial infarction presents with syncope without warning. His electrocardiogram shows bifascicular block.
stem: What is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: Syncope in the presence of conduction system disease suggests a potentially serious arrhythmic cause and warrants specialist cardiac evaluation.

sharedCase: A 63-year-old man with a history of myocardial infarction presents with syncope without warning. His electrocardiogram shows bifascicular block.
stem: Which findings indicate high risk syncope requiring aggressive investigation? Select ALL that apply.
explanation: Exertional syncope, structural heart disease, and family history of sudden death increase the likelihood of life-threatening causes.

vignette: A 70-year-old woman has recurrent syncope with documented complete heart block.
stem: What definitive therapy is indicated?
explanation: Syncope due to bradyarrhythmia or high-grade atrioventricular block requires permanent pacing.

sharedCase: A 70-year-old woman has recurrent syncope with documented complete heart block.
stem: Which therapies are appropriate for vasovagal syncope? Select ALL that apply

options.text: Increased dietary salt and fluid intake

explanation: Education, reassurance, volume expansion, and physical maneuvers are first-line therapies for vasovagal syncope.

vignette: A 61-year-old man with diabetes reports dizziness and syncope shortly after standing. Blood pressure drops by 25 mm Hg systolic on standing, with minimal heart rate increase.
stem: What is the most likely mechanism?
explanation: Orthostatic hypotension with absent compensatory tachycardia suggests autonomic failure, commonly seen in diabetes.

stem: Which statements regarding neuroimaging in syncope are correct? Select NONE

options.text: Neuroimaging identifies the cause in most patients
Neuroimaging is first-line in uncomplicated syncope

explanation: Routine neuroimaging is not recommended in the absence of focal neurologic findings or other concerning features.
