Posterior urethral valves are the most common cause of bladder outlet obstruction in newborn boys. The VCUG shows a dilated posterior urethra during voiding. Valves are removed endoscopically, with long-term kidney follow-up.

vignette: A 55-year-old man asks whether he should have a PSA test. He has no symptoms and no family history of prostate cancer.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: B
options.text: Discuss the benefits and harms and decide together

options.label: C
options.text: Order PSA every year starting now

options.label: D
options.text: Order a PSA only if digital rectal exam is abnormal

options.label: E
options.text: Tell him PSA screening is not recommended at any age

explanation: Shared decision-making.

For men aged 55–69, PSA screening offers a small reduction in prostate cancer deaths with real risks of false positives, biopsies, and overtreatment. The decision should follow a discussion of the patient's values. Screening is not recommended after 70.

vignette: A 64-year-old woman with obesity has 2 years of right knee pain that worsens with activity and improves with rest. Morning stiffness lasts 10 minutes. X-ray shows joint-space narrowing and bony spurs.
stem: Which of the following is the best initial management?
explanation: Exercise and weight loss.

Strengthening exercise and weight loss reduce pain and improve function in knee osteoarthritis. Topical NSAIDs, then oral NSAIDs or acetaminophen, are added for pain. Arthroscopy does not help osteoarthritis, and joint replacement is for advanced disease that fails other treatment.

vignette: A 61-year-old man has right shoulder pain and weakness after a fall. He cannot keep his arm raised to the side; when the examiner lifts it to 90° and lets go, the arm drops.
stem: Which muscle is most likely torn?
explanation: Supraspinatus.

The supraspinatus starts abduction and is the rotator cuff tendon most often torn. A positive drop-arm test suggests a full-thickness tear. MRI or ultrasound confirms; acute traumatic tears in active patients are often repaired.

vignette: A 43-year-old carpenter has pain on the outer elbow that worsens when he grips tools. There is tenderness just below the lateral epicondyle, and pain increases with resisted wrist extension.
stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Lateral epicondylitis.

"Tennis elbow" is overuse of the wrist extensors at their origin on the lateral epicondyle. Treatment is rest, activity change, a counterforce brace, NSAIDs, and physical therapy. Medial epicondylitis causes pain with resisted wrist flexion.

vignette: A 32-year-old woman with a 2-month-old baby has pain at the base of the thumb on the radial side of the wrist. Pain is reproduced when she makes a fist over her thumb and bends the wrist toward the little finger.
stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: De Quervain tenosynovitis.

It is inflammation of the tendons that move the thumb (abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis). It is common in new parents from lifting a baby. The Finkelstein test is positive. Treatment is a thumb spica splint, NSAIDs, or steroid injection.

vignette: A 13-year-old boy who plays basketball has pain and a tender bump just below the kneecap. Pain worsens with jumping and kneeling. X-ray shows fragmentation of the tibial tubercle.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
explanation: Rest, ice, activity change.
Osgood–Schlatter disease is traction injury where the patellar tendon pulls on the tibial tubercle during growth spurts. It resolves when growth ends. Pain guides activity; surgery is rarely needed.

vignette: A 3-week-old girl born in breech position has a clunk when the left hip is abducted and lifted forward.
stem: Which imaging study is most appropriate?
explanation: Hip ultrasound.

In infants under about 4–6 months, the femoral head is still cartilage and does not show on X-ray. Ultrasound shows how well the hip is seated. Developmental dysplasia is treated with a Pavlik harness when found early.

vignette: A 6-year-old boy has a painless limp for a month. Hip movement is limited, especially internal rotation and abduction. He has no fever. X-ray shows flattening and fragmentation of the left femoral head.
stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Legg–Calvé–Perthes disease.

This is avascular necrosis of the femoral head in children aged about 4–10, more often boys. It causes a painless or mildly painful limp. Treatment aims to keep the femoral head in the socket while it remodels.

vignette: A 5-year-old boy has a limp and right hip pain a week after a cold. He is afebrile and can bear weight. White count, ESR, and CRP are normal. Hip ultrasound shows a small effusion.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: B
options.text: NSAIDs and rest with close follow-up

explanation: NSAIDs and close follow-up.

Transient synovitis follows a viral illness in young children and settles in days. Septic arthritis is suggested by fever, refusal to bear weight, ESR above 40, and white count above 12,000 (Kocher criteria). With none of these, observation is appropriate.

vignette: A 6-year-old girl falls from monkey bars onto her outstretched arm. X-ray shows a displaced supracondylar fracture of the humerus.
stem: Which of the following must be assessed first?
explanation: Pulse and hand perfusion.

The brachial artery runs in front of the distal humerus and can be stretched or torn by a displaced supracondylar fracture. Vascular injury can lead to compartment syndrome and Volkmann contracture. The median nerve (especially the anterior interosseous branch) is also checked.

vignette: A 2-year-old girl stopped using her right arm after her father pulled her up by the hand. She holds the arm slightly bent and turned palm-down, and there is no swelling or deformity.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: D
options.text: Reduction by turning the forearm fully palm-down

explanation: Reduce without X-ray.

Radial head subluxation ("nursemaid's elbow") follows a pull on the arm in a toddler. With a typical story and no swelling, no X-ray is needed. Hyperpronation of the forearm, or turning it palm-up and bending the elbow, reduces it; the child usually uses the arm within minutes.

vignette: An 82-year-old woman falls at home. Her right leg is shortened and turned outward, and X-ray shows a displaced femoral neck fracture. She was walking independently before the fall.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.label: B
options.text: Bed rest and traction for 6 weeks

explanation: Hip arthroplasty.

A displaced femoral neck fracture disrupts the blood supply to the femoral head, so screw fixation often fails in older adults. Replacement (hemi- or total arthroplasty) within 24–48 hours allows early walking and reduces complications.

vignette: A 35-year-old man's knee hit the dashboard in a car crash. His right leg is shortened, bent, turned inward, and pulled toward the midline. X-ray shows a posterior hip dislocation without fracture.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: Urgent closed reduction.
Posterior hip dislocation is an emergency. Reduction within about 6 hours reduces the risk of avascular necrosis of the femoral head. The sciatic nerve is checked before and after reduction.

vignette: A 44-year-old man felt a pop at the back of his ankle while playing tennis, as if he had been kicked. He has trouble pushing off. Squeezing his calf while he lies face down does not flex the foot.
stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Achilles tendon rupture.

A sudden pop during push-off, typically in middle-aged men playing sports, with a positive Thompson test (no plantar flexion when the calf is squeezed). Treatment is functional bracing or surgical repair.

vignette: A 24-year-old woman twisted her ankle stepping off a curb. She walked four steps in the clinic with a limp. She has swelling and tenderness in front of the lateral malleolus but no tenderness over the back edge or tip of either malleolus or the base of the fifth metatarsal.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.text: Rest, ice, compression, elevation, and early movement

explanation: RICE and early movement.

The Ottawa ankle rules say X-rays are needed only for bone tenderness at the posterior edge or tip of either malleolus, at the base of the fifth metatarsal or the navicular, or inability to bear weight for four steps. She has none, so this is a sprain.

vignette: A 58-year-old man with diabetes has an ulcer on the ball of his foot for 2 months. A sterile metal probe touches bone at the base of the ulcer. X-ray is normal.
stem: Which test is best to confirm the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: MRI of the foot.

Being able to probe to bone in a diabetic foot ulcer strongly suggests osteomyelitis. X-ray changes take about 2 weeks to appear. MRI is the most accurate imaging test; bone biopsy gives the organism.

vignette: A 39-year-old man has low back pain spreading down the back of his left leg to the outer foot. Examination shows a reduced left ankle reflex.
stem: Which nerve root is most likely compressed?
explanation: The S1 root supplies the ankle reflex, foot plantar flexion, and sensation over the lateral foot and sole. L5 causes weak big-toe extension and foot dorsiflexion with numbness on the top of the foot; L4 affects the knee reflex.

vignette: A 72-year-old man has pain and heaviness in both legs when he walks or stands for long, relieved by sitting or bending forward, as when leaning on a shopping cart. Foot pulses are normal.
stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Lumbar spinal stenosis.

Narrowing of the spinal canal causes leg pain with standing and walking (neurogenic claudication), relieved by flexing forward, which widens the canal. In vascular claudication, standing still relieves pain and pulses are reduced. MRI confirms.

vignette: A 41-year-old man who injects drugs has 3 weeks of worsening back pain and fevers. There is tenderness when the lower thoracic spine is tapped. ESR is 98 mm/h.
stem: Which of the following is the best test?

options.label: A
options.text: MRI of the spine with contrast

explanation: MRI with contrast.

Fever, back pain, and spinal tenderness in someone who injects drugs suggest vertebral osteomyelitis or epidural abscess. MRI is the most sensitive test. Blood cultures are drawn and Staphylococcus aureus is the usual cause.

vignette: A 15-year-old boy has 2 months of pain above the knee that wakes him at night. X-ray of the distal femur shows a destructive lesion with a sunburst pattern and lifting of the bone's outer layer.
stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Osteosarcoma.

It is the most common primary bone cancer in adolescents and usually arises near the knee in the metaphysis. X-ray shows a sunburst pattern and Codman triangle. Ewing sarcoma tends to affect the diaphysis with an onion-skin pattern.

vignette: A 22-year-old man punched a wall. The knuckle of his little finger is depressed and swollen. X-ray shows a fracture of the neck of the fifth metacarpal with mild angulation and no rotation. There is no skin break.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.label: C
options.text: Buddy taping and return to sport today

explanation: Ulnar gutter splint.

A "boxer's fracture" with mild angulation and no rotation is treated with a splint. Rotational deformity or marked angulation needs reduction. Any wound over the knuckle is assumed to be a human bite and needs washout and antibiotics.

vignette: A 52-year-old woman has a melanoma removed from her calf.
stem: Which feature of the pathology report best predicts her prognosis?
explanation: Breslow thickness.

The depth of invasion, measured in millimeters from the top of the granular layer, is the strongest predictor of survival in localized melanoma and determines margins and the need for sentinel node biopsy. Ulceration and mitotic rate also matter.

vignette: A 66-year-old man has developed dozens of waxy, "stuck-on" brown papules over his trunk within 2 months. He has also lost 7 kg.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: E
options.text: Evaluation for internal cancer, especially of the stomach

explanation: Look for internal cancer.

Sudden eruption of many seborrheic keratoses (the sign of Leser–Trélat) is a rare sign of internal cancer, most often gastric adenocarcinoma. Weight loss adds to the concern. Ordinary seborrheic keratoses are benign and need no treatment.

vignette: A 15-year-old girl with obesity has velvety, darkened skin on the back of her neck and in her armpits.
stem: Which test is most appropriate?
explanation: Fasting glucose or HbA1c.

Acanthosis nigricans most commonly signals insulin resistance (obesity, prediabetes, type 2 diabetes, polycystic ovary syndrome). Sudden, extensive acanthosis in a thin older adult raises concern for gastric cancer.

vignette: A 23-year-old man has many pale, finely scaling spots on his upper back and chest that became noticeable after a summer tan. A potassium hydroxide preparation shows short hyphae and round yeast.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation: Topical selenium sulfide or ketoconazole.

Tinea versicolor is caused by Malassezia yeast. The patches do not tan, so they show after sun exposure. The "spaghetti and meatballs" appearance on KOH is typical. It often recurs, so periodic preventive treatment is used.

vignette: A 30-year-old woman has intense itching, worse at night, with small papules and short wavy lines between her fingers and on her wrists. Her husband and son are also itchy.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.label: B
options.text: Topical permethrin for the patient only

options.label: D
options.text: Topical permethrin for the patient and all household contacts

options.label: E
options.text: Topical corticosteroid for the patient only

explanation: Permethrin for everyone in the house.

Scabies spreads through close contact. All household members are treated at the same time, even without symptoms, and clothing and bedding are washed hot. Itching can last weeks after successful treatment.

vignette: A 5-year-old boy has a few honey-colored crusted sores around his nose and mouth. He is otherwise well.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation: Topical mupirocin.

Limited impetigo is treated with a topical antibiotic. Oral antibiotics are for extensive disease, outbreaks, or bullous impetigo. Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes are the usual causes.

vignette: A 22-year-old sexually active man has a single oval scaly patch on his trunk, followed a week later by many smaller oval patches along the skin lines of his back. Palms and soles are clear.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: Rapid plasma reagin test.

Pityriasis rosea starts with a herald patch and then a "Christmas tree" rash and resolves on its own in 6–8 weeks. Secondary syphilis can look similar, so a sexually active patient should be tested, especially if palms or soles are involved.

vignette: A 40-year-old woman has facial flushing triggered by hot drinks and alcohol, with red papules and pustules on her cheeks and nose. There are no blackheads.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation: Topical metronidazole.

Rosacea causes flushing, redness, and papules and pustules without comedones, which separates it from acne. Topical metronidazole, azelaic acid, or ivermectin is first-line; oral doxycycline is used for more severe cases. Avoiding triggers helps.

vignette: A 28-year-old woman has tender red nodules on both shins, fever, and ankle pain.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: Chest X-ray.

Erythema nodosum is inflammation of fat under the skin linked to streptococcal infection, sarcoidosis, inflammatory bowel disease, drugs, and pregnancy. Fever, ankle pain, and erythema nodosum suggest Löfgren syndrome, so a chest X-ray looks for enlarged hilar lymph nodes.

vignette: A 35-year-old man with ulcerative colitis has a rapidly growing painful ulcer on his leg with a purple, overhanging edge. It began as a small pustule after a minor injury.
stem: Which of the following should be avoided?
explanation: Surgical debridement.

Pyoderma gangrenosum worsens with injury (pathergy), so cutting it makes it bigger. It is associated with inflammatory bowel disease, arthritis, and blood cancers. Treatment is systemic steroids or other immunosuppressants and good wound care.

vignette: A 34-year-old woman has had itchy hives that come and go daily for 4 months. Each wheal lasts under 24 hours. There is no swelling of the lips or throat and no clear trigger.
stem: Which of the following is the best initial treatment?

options.label: C
options.text: Daily second-generation antihistamine such as cetirizine

explanation: Second-generation antihistamine.

Chronic hives (over 6 weeks) usually have no identifiable cause. A non-sedating antihistamine taken daily is first-line and can be increased up to four times the usual dose. Omalizumab is used if this fails. Extensive testing is rarely helpful.

vignette: A 26-year-old woman has an itchy, scaling rash on her lower abdomen exactly where her belt buckle rests.
stem: Which test best confirms the cause?
explanation: Patch testing.
Allergic contact dermatitis is a delayed (type IV) reaction; nickel is the most common cause. Patch testing reproduces delayed reactions. Skin prick testing detects immediate (IgE) allergy.

vignette: A 68-year-old man with Parkinson disease has greasy yellow scaling on his scalp, eyebrows, and the folds beside his nose.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation: Topical ketoconazole.
Seborrheic dermatitis is linked to Malassezia yeast and is more common and severe in Parkinson disease and HIV. Antifungal shampoos or creams, with short courses of mild topical steroid, control it.

vignette: A 32-year-old man has dozens of small, flesh-colored, dome-shaped papules with central dimples on his face and beard area.
stem: Which test is most appropriate?
explanation: HIV test.
Molluscum contagiosum is common and harmless in children. Many lesions on the face of an adult, especially large or widespread ones, suggest weakened immunity, most often from HIV.

vignette: A 27-year-old woman has intensely itchy clusters of small blisters on her elbows, knees, and buttocks. She has bloating and loose stools.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment in addition to dapsone?
explanation: Gluten-free diet.

Dermatitis herpetiformis is the skin form of celiac disease, with IgA deposits in the tips of the dermal papillae. Dapsone controls itching quickly, and a strict gluten-free diet treats the cause and lowers lymphoma risk.

vignette: A 30-year-old woman has well-defined, completely depigmented patches around her mouth and on her hands.
stem: Which condition should be checked for?
explanation: Autoimmune thyroid disease.
Vitiligo is autoimmune destruction of pigment cells and often occurs with autoimmune thyroid disease, type 1 diabetes, pernicious anemia, and Addison disease. Checking TSH is reasonable.

vignette: A 56-year-old man has a chronic ulcer that has grown over a scar from a burn he had 30 years ago. The edges are raised and hard.
stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Squamous cell carcinoma.
A cancer arising in an old burn scar or chronic wound is called a Marjolin ulcer and is usually squamous cell carcinoma. It tends to be aggressive. Any non-healing ulcer in a scar should be biopsied.

vignette: A 3-month-old girl has a bright red, raised, growing birthmark on her upper eyelid that is starting to close the eye.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.label: C
options.text: Observation until it shrinks on its own

explanation: Oral propranolol.
Most infantile hemangiomas grow for months and then shrink. Treatment is needed when they threaten function: near the eye they can cause amblyopia. Propranolol is first-line for problem hemangiomas.

vignette: A 52-year-old man has fever and severe pain in his thigh, out of proportion to mild redness. Over 6 hours the redness spreads, the skin becomes dusky, and crepitus is felt.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: Emergency surgery.

Necrotizing fasciitis spreads along fascia quickly. Pain out of proportion, rapid spread, dusky skin, and crepitus mean surgery is needed at once, with broad IV antibiotics including clindamycin. Imaging must not delay the operation.

vignette: A 25-year-old man has a 3-cm red, warm, tender swelling on his thigh that is soft and fluctuant in the center. He is afebrile and otherwise well.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation: Incision and drainage.
A fluctuant abscess needs drainage; antibiotics alone cannot clear the pus. Antibiotics covering MRSA are added for large abscesses, fever, cellulitis around it, or weakened immunity.

vignette: A 55-year-old man has had three attacks of gout in the past year. His current attack resolved 2 weeks ago. Uric acid is 9.4 mg/dL and kidney function is normal.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term plan?

options.label: C
options.text: Allopurinol, with low-dose colchicine for the first months

explanation: Allopurinol with colchicine prophylaxis.

Urate-lowering therapy is started after two or more attacks a year, tophi, or urate kidney stones, aiming for uric acid below 6 mg/dL. Starting it can trigger attacks, so low-dose colchicine or an NSAID is given for the first 3–6 months. Testing for HLA-B*58:01 is advised in people of Southeast Asian or African descent before allopurinol.

vignette: A 26-year-old woman with lupus is being monitored.
stem: Which test best reflects activity of lupus kidney disease?
explanation: Anti-dsDNA and complement.
Anti-dsDNA levels rise and C3 and C4 fall when lupus, especially lupus nephritis, is active. ANA is used for screening, not monitoring. Anti-Smith is very specific but does not track activity.

vignette: A 24-year-old woman with lupus has new swelling of the legs. Urine shows red cell casts and 3 g of protein a day. Kidney biopsy shows diffuse proliferative lupus nephritis (class IV).
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation: Steroids with mycophenolate.

Class III and IV lupus nephritis are the most serious types and need intensive treatment: glucocorticoids plus mycophenolate or cyclophosphamide. Hydroxychloroquine is continued in all lupus patients.

vignette: A 33-year-old woman with lupus has taken hydroxychloroquine for 6 years.
stem: Which regular examination is required?
explanation: Retinal eye examination.
Hydroxychloroquine can damage the retina. A baseline exam is done, then yearly screening after 5 years (sooner with risk factors such as kidney disease or high dose).

vignette: A 48-year-old woman has dry eyes, dry mouth, and swollen parotid glands. Anti-Ro (SSA) and anti-La (SSB) antibodies are positive.
stem: Which cancer is she at increased risk of?
explanation: B-cell lymphoma.
Sjögren syndrome carries a much higher risk of non-Hodgkin lymphoma, often of the parotid gland (MALT type). Persistent gland swelling, low complement, and cryoglobulins are warning signs.

vignette: A 31-year-old pregnant woman is known to have anti-Ro antibodies.
stem: Which complication in the baby is she at risk of?
explanation: Congenital heart block.

Maternal anti-Ro antibodies cross the placenta and can damage the baby's heart conduction system. Fetal heart rate is monitored between about 16 and 26 weeks. The baby can also have a lupus-like rash.

vignette: A 54-year-old woman has trouble climbing stairs and lifting her arms. She has a purple rash on her eyelids and scaly red bumps over her knuckles. Creatine kinase is high.
stem: Which of the following is the most important next step after confirming the diagnosis?
explanation: Screen for cancer.

Dermatomyositis is linked to cancers including ovarian, lung, stomach, colon, and lymphoma, especially in the first few years. Age-appropriate screening plus targeted imaging is done. Treatment is glucocorticoids with a steroid-sparing drug.

vignette: A 24-year-old man has painful urination, red eyes, and a swollen right knee and left ankle 3 weeks after unprotected sex. Joint fluid culture is negative.
stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Reactive arthritis.

It follows chlamydia or gut infections (Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, Yersinia) by 1–4 weeks, with asymmetric arthritis of large leg joints, eye inflammation, and urethritis. Joint fluid is sterile. NSAIDs are first-line; HLA-B27 is often positive.

vignette: A 42-year-old man with psoriasis has a swollen "sausage" finger and pain in the joints nearest his fingertips.
stem: Which X-ray finding is most typical?

options.label: D
options.text: Bony spurs at the middle finger joints

explanation: Pencil-in-cup deformity.

Psoriatic arthritis affects the distal joints, causes dactylitis and nail pitting, and erodes bone so the end of one bone looks like a pencil in a cup. Punched-out erosions with overhanging edges suggest gout.

vignette: A 38-year-old woman has widespread pain for a year, poor sleep, fatigue, and many tender points. Joints are not swollen, and blood count, ESR, CK, and TSH are normal.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.label: A
options.text: Graded aerobic exercise, with duloxetine if needed

explanation: Exercise and duloxetine.

Fibromyalgia is managed with education, graded aerobic exercise, sleep hygiene, and cognitive behavioral therapy. Duloxetine, milnacipran, pregabalin, or low-dose amitriptyline may help. Opioids and steroids do not.

vignette: A 21-year-old sexually active woman has fever, joint pain moving from joint to joint, pain along tendons of her wrists, and a few small pustules on her hands.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation: IV ceftriaxone.
Disseminated gonococcal infection causes the triad of migrating joint pain, tenosynovitis, and skin pustules. Treatment is ceftriaxone, plus doxycycline for chlamydia unless it is excluded.

vignette: A 30-year-old man of Turkish descent has recurrent painful mouth ulcers, genital ulcers, and eye inflammation. A pustule forms at the site of a needle prick.
stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Behçet disease.

It is a vasculitis common along the old Silk Road. It causes recurrent mouth and genital ulcers, uveitis, and pathergy (a pustule after skin prick). Colchicine and steroids are used, with stronger immunosuppression for eye or nervous system involvement.

vignette: A 27-year-old Japanese woman has arm fatigue when using her hands, dizziness, and weight loss. Radial pulses are weak, and blood pressure is 30 mm Hg lower in the left arm.
stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Takayasu arteritis.

It is inflammation of the aorta and its main branches, mostly in young Asian women. It causes weak pulses, arm claudication, and different blood pressures between arms ("pulseless disease"). Steroids are first-line.

vignette: A 3-year-old boy has had fever for 6 days, red eyes without discharge, cracked red lips, a red tongue, a rash, swollen hands and feet, and a large neck lymph node.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation: IV immunoglobulin and aspirin.

Kawasaki disease is fever for 5 days or more with four of five signs: conjunctivitis, mouth changes, rash, swollen hands and feet, and a neck lymph node. IVIG given within 10 days reduces coronary aneurysms. An echocardiogram is done at diagnosis.

vignette: A 50-year-old man with chronic hepatitis B has hypertension, abdominal pain after eating, and foot drop. Kidney arteries show small aneurysms on angiography. His lungs are normal.
stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Polyarteritis nodosa.
It affects medium-sized arteries in the kidney, gut, nerves, and skin, with aneurysms on angiography. It is associated with hepatitis B, is ANCA-negative, and spares the lungs.

vignette: A 6-year-old boy has raised purple spots on his buttocks and legs, abdominal pain, and knee pain a week after a sore throat. Platelets are normal.
stem: Which complication must be watched for?
explanation: Intussusception.

IgA vasculitis (Henoch–Schönlein purpura) causes palpable purpura with normal platelets, abdominal pain, arthritis, and sometimes kidney disease. Swelling of the bowel wall can lead to intussusception. Urinalysis and blood pressure are followed for months.

vignette: A 46-year-old woman is starting methotrexate for rheumatoid arthritis.
stem: Which supplement should be added?
explanation: Folic acid.

Methotrexate blocks folate metabolism. Folic acid reduces mouth ulcers, nausea, liver enzyme rises, and low blood counts without reducing benefit. Blood count, liver tests, and creatinine are checked regularly.

vignette: A 39-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis not controlled on methotrexate is going to start a TNF inhibitor.
stem: Which test is required first?
explanation: Latent tuberculosis screening.

TNF is needed to keep tuberculosis walled off in granulomas, so TNF inhibitors can reactivate latent TB. A TB skin test or interferon-gamma release assay is done first, along with hepatitis B testing.

vignette: A 70-year-old woman has hard bony swellings at the joints nearest her fingertips, with mild morning stiffness that lasts 10 minutes. ESR and rheumatoid factor are normal.
stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Osteoarthritis.

Bony enlargement of the distal finger joints (Heberden nodes) and middle joints (Bouchard nodes) with brief stiffness is typical of osteoarthritis. Rheumatoid arthritis spares the distal joints and causes soft swelling and long morning stiffness.

vignette: A 52-year-old woman has had Raynaud phenomenon for years, tight skin on her fingers, small dilated blood vessels on her face, and difficulty swallowing. Anti-centromere antibody is positive.
stem: Which complication is she at greatest risk of?

options.label: E
options.text: Sudden kidney failure with severe hypertension

explanation: Pulmonary arterial hypertension.

Limited systemic sclerosis (CREST: calcinosis, Raynaud, esophageal problems, sclerodactyly, telangiectasia) is linked to anti-centromere antibodies and to pulmonary hypertension. Yearly echocardiograms and lung function tests are recommended. Kidney crisis is more typical of the diffuse form.

vignette: A 5-month-old boy has severe eczema. His parents ask about introducing peanut.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate advice?

options.label: A
options.text: Allergy evaluation now, then early introduction of peanut-containing food if appropriate

options.label: E
options.text: Mother should avoid peanut while breastfeeding

explanation: Evaluate, then introduce peanut early.

Infants with severe eczema or egg allergy are at high risk of peanut allergy. Introducing peanut at around 4–6 months, after evaluation for existing allergy, greatly reduces the chance of developing it. Delaying peanut increases risk.

vignette: A 45-year-old woman needs treatment for syphilis. She reports that 20 years ago she had hives within an hour of taking penicillin. There are no other treatment options for her.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: B
options.text: Give penicillin with an antihistamine beforehand

options.label: D
options.text: Avoid all beta-lactams for life without testing

explanation: Penicillin skin testing.

Most people labeled penicillin-allergic are not allergic now; IgE allergy fades over years. With a history of immediate hives and penicillin needed, skin testing followed by an oral challenge, or desensitization if positive, is the route. Premedication does not prevent anaphylaxis.

vignette: A 2-year-old boy has eczema, recurrent ear infections, and bloody diarrhea. Platelets are 40,000/mm³ and are small on the blood film.
stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome.

It is an X-linked disorder with eczema, low platelets that are small, and recurrent infections, caused by WAS gene mutations. It carries a raised risk of autoimmune disease and lymphoma; stem cell transplant is curative.

vignette: A 5-month-old girl has chronic diarrhea, failure to gain weight, persistent oral thrush, and Pneumocystis pneumonia. Lymphocyte count is very low and no thymus is seen on chest X-ray.
stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Severe combined immunodeficiency.

Absent T cells (and functionally absent B cells) cause severe infections in the first months, chronic diarrhea, thrush, and Pneumocystis. No thymic shadow is seen. Newborn screening (TREC assay) detects it. Live vaccines are avoided and stem cell transplant is needed.

vignette: A 3-year-old boy has had recurrent sinus and lung infections and Pneumocystis pneumonia. IgM is high, and IgG, IgA, and IgE are very low.
stem: Which defect is most likely?
explanation: CD40 ligand.

Without CD40 ligand on helper T cells, B cells cannot switch from making IgM to other classes. Hyper-IgM syndrome causes recurrent bacterial infections and opportunistic ones such as Pneumocystis and Cryptosporidium.

vignette: A 7-year-old girl has eczema, recurrent skin abscesses that are not warm or red, repeated lung infections, and baby teeth that have not fallen out. IgE is extremely high.
stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Hyper-IgE syndrome.

Usually from STAT3 mutation (Job syndrome): eczema, "cold" staphylococcal abscesses without warmth or redness, recurrent pneumonia with cavities, retained baby teeth, coarse facial features, and very high IgE.

vignette: A 19-year-old man has his second episode of meningococcal meningitis.
stem: Which test is most likely to reveal the cause?
explanation: CH50.

Recurrent Neisseria infections suggest deficiency of the terminal complement components (C5–C9) that form the membrane attack complex. CH50 is a screening test; it is low when any classical pathway component is missing.

vignette: A 4-year-old boy has light skin and silvery hair, recurrent pyogenic infections, and numbness in his feet. The blood film shows giant granules in neutrophils.
stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Chediak–Higashi syndrome.
A defect in lysosomal trafficking (LYST gene) causes giant granules in white cells, partial albinism, nerve damage, bleeding, and recurrent infections.

vignette: A 3-week-old boy's umbilical cord has not fallen off. He has a skin infection without pus and a white count of 45,000/mm³.
stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency.
White cells lack CD18 integrins and cannot leave the bloodstream, so counts are very high but no pus forms at infection sites. Delayed separation of the umbilical cord is a classic early sign.

vignette: A 34-year-old woman with asthma has worsening wheeze and cough with brown mucus plugs. Eosinophils and IgE are very high, and skin testing to Aspergillus is positive. CT shows widened central airways.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation: Prednisone with itraconazole.

Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis is a hypersensitivity reaction to Aspergillus in people with asthma or cystic fibrosis. Steroids reduce inflammation and itraconazole reduces the fungal load. Untreated, it causes central bronchiectasis.

vignette: A 28-year-old man started carbamazepine 4 weeks ago. He now has fever, a widespread rash, facial swelling, enlarged lymph nodes, eosinophilia, and raised liver enzymes.
stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.label: A
options.text: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms

explanation: DRESS.

Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms starts 2–8 weeks after a drug such as an anticonvulsant, allopurinol, or sulfonamide. It causes fever, rash, facial swelling, eosinophilia, and organ damage, often to the liver. The drug is stopped and systemic steroids are often needed.

vignette: A 26-year-old woman with spring hay fever gets an itchy mouth and throat within minutes of eating a raw apple. Baked apple pie causes no symptoms.
stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Oral allergy syndrome.
Antibodies to birch pollen cross-react with similar proteins in raw fruits such as apples. Cooking destroys these proteins. Symptoms are usually limited to the mouth.

vignette: A 32-year-old nurse has hives and wheezing after wearing gloves. She asks which foods she should be careful with.
stem: Which group of foods is most associated with her allergy?
explanation: Banana, avocado, and kiwi.
Latex proteins cross-react with proteins in banana, avocado, kiwi, and chestnut (the latex-fruit syndrome). Latex-allergic patients need latex-free gloves and equipment.

vignette: A 60-year-old man needs a CT scan with IV contrast. He had hives after contrast 3 years ago.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate step?
explanation: Premedicate.

For a past mild to moderate reaction to contrast, guidelines recommend premedication with a corticosteroid (such as prednisone 13, 7, and 1 hour before) and an antihistamine, or choosing a different contrast agent. Seafood allergy does not predict contrast reactions.

vignette: A 30-year-old woman with egg allergy that causes hives asks whether she can have the influenza vaccine.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.text: She needs two half doses a month apart

options.label: B
options.text: She can receive any age-appropriate influenza vaccine

options.label: C
options.text: She should never receive the influenza vaccine

options.label: D
options.text: She needs skin testing to the vaccine first

options.label: E
options.text: She can only receive it in an intensive care unit

explanation: Any age-appropriate influenza vaccine.
Current influenza vaccines contain very little egg protein. People with egg allergy of any severity can receive them in the usual setting without extra precautions.

vignette: A 22-year-old man had his spleen removed after a car crash.
stem: Which vaccines are most important?

options.label: D
options.text: Pneumococcal, meningococcal, and Haemophilus influenzae type b

explanation: Pneumococcal, meningococcal, and Hib.

The spleen clears encapsulated bacteria. People without one are at risk of overwhelming infection with Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, and Haemophilus influenzae. Annual influenza vaccine is also advised.

vignette: A 25-year-old health care worker has a tuberculin skin test. The area becomes hard and raised 48 hours later.
stem: Which type of immune reaction is this?
explanation: Type IV, delayed.
The tuberculin reaction is driven by memory T cells that recruit macrophages over 48–72 hours. Contact dermatitis is also type IV.

vignette: A 28-year-old woman with Rh-negative blood is 28 weeks pregnant. The father is Rh-positive. Antibody screen is negative.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate step?
explanation: Anti-D immunoglobulin.
Giving anti-D at 28 weeks, and again within 72 hours after delivery of an Rh-positive baby, prevents the mother from forming anti-D antibodies that would attack red cells in future pregnancies.

vignette: A 41-year-old beekeeper had hives, throat tightness, and fainting after a bee sting last month.
stem: Which of the following most reduces his risk of another severe reaction?
explanation: Venom immunotherapy.
For adults with a systemic reaction to an insect sting, venom immunotherapy reduces the risk of future anaphylaxis from about 60% to under 5%. An epinephrine autoinjector is also prescribed.

vignette: A 62-year-old man with no family history develops episodes of swelling of the face and tongue without hives. He is not taking an ACE inhibitor. C4 and C1q are both low.
stem: Which condition should be looked for?
explanation: Lymphoma.

Acquired C1 inhibitor deficiency appears later in life without family history, usually with B-cell lymphoproliferative disease or autoantibodies to C1 inhibitor. Low C1q separates it from hereditary angioedema, in which C1q is normal.

vignette: A 48-year-old man has waited 90 minutes past his appointment time. When the physician enters, he says angrily, "My time is valuable too."
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.text: "I'm sorry you had such a long wait, and I understand why you're frustrated."

options.label: B
options.text: Say nothing and begin the history

options.label: D
options.text: "If you're unhappy, you can see another doctor."

options.label: E
options.text: "We had several emergencies this morning, so it couldn't be helped."

explanation: Apologize and acknowledge his feelings.
Naming the emotion and apologizing for the wait defuses anger and shows respect. Explanations or excuses given first can feel dismissive. Once he feels heard, the visit can move forward.

vignette: A 31-year-old woman has 3 days of runny nose, sore throat, and cough. She has no fever and examination is normal. She asks for an antibiotic because "it always works for me."
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: B
options.text: Ask about her concerns, explain why antibiotics will not help, and discuss symptom relief

options.label: C
options.text: Refer her to an infectious disease specialist

options.label: D
options.text: Give a delayed prescription without discussion

options.label: E
options.text: Prescribe azithromycin to keep her satisfied

explanation: Explore, explain, and offer relief.

Antibiotics do not help viral infections and cause side effects and resistance. Understanding what she hopes for, explaining clearly, and offering a plan for symptoms usually satisfies patients more than an unnecessary prescription.

vignette: A grateful 70-year-old patient whose cancer is in remission gives his oncologist a check for $500 as a personal thank-you.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.text: Thank him warmly and decline the money

options.label: B
options.text: Accept it and donate it to charity without telling the patient

options.label: C
options.text: Accept it if he is not a current patient

options.label: E
options.text: Ask him to give cash instead

explanation: Decline money politely.
Small, inexpensive gifts may be accepted. Cash or large gifts can change the relationship and create a sense of obligation and should be declined with thanks.

vignette: A resident's friend is admitted to the hospital. A colleague asks the resident to look at the friend's chart "just to see how she's doing." The resident is not involved in her care.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask the patient's nurse to share the information instead

options.label: B
options.text: Look at the chart but share only general information

options.label: C
options.text: Look at it since they are friends

options.label: D
options.text: Decline, because looking at the chart without a role in her care is not permitted

options.label: E
options.text: Ask the hospital's IT department for permission

explanation: Decline.

Privacy rules allow access to records only for people involved in a patient's care or with another legitimate purpose. Looking at a friend's chart out of curiosity is a privacy breach, even with good intentions.

vignette: During a session, a 34-year-old man tells his psychiatrist he plans to kill his former business partner and names him. He has access to a gun.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate action?

options.label: B
options.text: Document the statement and see him in a week

options.label: C
options.text: Wait to see whether he repeats the threat

options.label: E
options.text: Take steps to protect the named person, such as warning him or notifying police

explanation: Protect the person threatened.

When a patient makes a serious threat of violence against an identifiable person, the duty to protect (the Tarasoff principle) outweighs confidentiality. Steps include warning the person, notifying police, or hospitalizing the patient.

vignette: A 24-year-old man is diagnosed with gonorrhea. He asks the physician not to tell anyone, including the health department.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.text: Explain that the infection must be reported to the health department, and encourage him to tell his partners

options.label: B
options.text: Call his partners yourself without telling him

options.label: E
options.text: Report it only if he does not return for follow-up

explanation: Report and encourage partner notification.

Gonorrhea, chlamydia, syphilis, HIV, and other diseases must be reported to public health by law. The physician explains this and encourages the patient to inform partners or use health department partner services.

vignette: A 38-year-old man has a new diagnosis of HIV. He refuses to tell his wife and says he will keep having unprotected sex with her. Despite counseling, he will not change his mind.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Respect his wishes and keep the information confidential

options.label: B
options.text: Refuse to continue his HIV care

options.label: D
options.text: Tell his wife at her next routine visit without telling him

options.label: E
options.text: Notify the health department or partner notification program as the law allows

explanation: Health department or partner notification.

The physician first tries to persuade the patient. If he still refuses and a partner is at clear risk, most jurisdictions allow or require notification through public health. Care for the patient continues.

vignette: A 79-year-old man is unconscious after a stroke and cannot make decisions. He has no advance directive or appointed proxy. His wife wants comfort care only, and his adult son wants full treatment.
stem: Who is the appropriate decision-maker?
explanation: The wife.

When there is no advance directive or appointed proxy, most states follow an order of surrogates: spouse, then adult children, then parents, then siblings. The surrogate should decide based on what the patient would have wanted.

vignette: A 16-year-old girl who is 10 weeks pregnant comes to the clinic alone for prenatal care. She does not want her parents involved.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate action?

options.label: A
options.text: Wait until she is 18 weeks so a court can decide

options.label: B
options.text: Refer her to a social worker before any care is given

options.label: D
options.text: Require parental consent before any care

options.label: E
options.text: Provide prenatal care with her consent

explanation: Provide care.
Pregnant minors can consent to their own pregnancy-related care in most states. The physician encourages her to involve a trusted adult but does not require it.

vignette: A 35-year-old man is brought in unconscious after a motorcycle crash with a ruptured spleen. No family can be reached and there is no identification.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate action?

options.label: A
options.text: Give only IV fluids until he wakes up

options.label: B
options.text: Ask two nurses to sign as witnesses before deciding

options.label: D
options.text: Seek a court order before surgery

options.label: E
options.text: Wait until family can be found

explanation: Proceed with surgery.
In an emergency, when the patient cannot consent and no surrogate is available, consent is implied and life-saving treatment is given.

vignette: A third-year medical student is asked by a busy resident to place a central line alone. The student has never placed one and has not been trained.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.text: Explain that he has not been trained and ask for supervision

options.label: B
options.text: Report the resident to the dean immediately

options.label: C
options.text: Tell the patient a doctor is placing it

options.label: D
options.text: Attempt the procedure and call for help if there is a problem

options.label: E
options.text: Watch a video and then attempt it

explanation: Ask for supervision.
Trainees should not do procedures they are not trained for without supervision. Patient safety comes first, and the patient must be told accurately who is doing the procedure.

vignette: A 68-year-old man with metastatic cancer asks his physician to prescribe pills that he could take to end his life.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate first response?

options.label: C
options.text: Admit him to a psychiatric unit

options.label: D
options.text: Tell him this is illegal and change the subject

options.label: E
options.text: Ask him what is leading him to feel this way

explanation: Explore his reasons.

Requests for hastened death often come from uncontrolled pain, depression, fear of being a burden, or loss of control. Understanding and addressing these is the first step, whatever the local law on physician-assisted death.

vignette: A 59-year-old woman with ALS on a ventilator has full decision-making capacity. She asks that the ventilator be removed, knowing she will die.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate action?

options.label: C
options.text: Wait 6 months to confirm her wishes

options.label: D
options.text: Honor her request and provide medication for comfort

options.label: E
options.text: Refuse, because stopping a treatment is different from not starting it

explanation: Honor her request.

A patient with capacity may refuse or stop any treatment, including life support. Withdrawing a treatment is ethically equivalent to not starting it. Sedatives and opioids for comfort are appropriate.

vignette: A pharmaceutical company representative invites a physician and her spouse on an all-expenses-paid weekend at a resort to hear a talk about a new drug.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: B
options.text: Accept if the drug is one she already prescribes

options.label: C
options.text: Accept, as long as she attends the talk

options.label: D
options.text: Accept, but pay for her spouse

options.label: E
options.text: Accept and disclose it to patients

explanation: Decline.

Lavish gifts and paid trips from industry create conflicts of interest and influence prescribing. Modest educational materials and gifts that benefit patients may be acceptable; travel and leisure for physicians and spouses are not.

vignette: A 42-year-old patient sends her physician a friend request on a social media site.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.text: Accept and then remove her after a month

options.label: D
options.text: Politely decline and keep communication through professional channels

options.label: E
options.text: Accept, but avoid discussing health online

explanation: Decline politely.
Personal social media relationships with patients blur professional boundaries and risk privacy breaches. Communication should stay within secure, professional channels.

vignette: A physician begins an interview with a new patient.
stem: Which of the following is the best way to start?

options.label: C
options.text: "Are you here for your blood pressure?"

explanation: An open-ended question.
Open questions let patients tell their story in their own words and bring up their main concerns. Closed questions are used later to fill in details.

vignette: A 55-year-old man's blood pressure remains high on three medications. Pharmacy records show he refills them only every other month.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask in a non-judgmental way about any difficulties taking his medications

options.label: E
options.text: Tell him he is not taking his pills

explanation: Ask non-judgmentally about barriers.

Before adding drugs, check whether he is taking the current ones. Cost, side effects, confusion, or beliefs may be the cause. A respectful, open question, such as "Many people have trouble taking pills every day," gets honest answers.

vignette: An 84-year-old woman with mild dementia lives with her son. She has bruises of different ages on her upper arms, is underweight, and seems afraid when her son speaks. She denies any problem.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate action?

options.label: A
options.text: Schedule a follow-up visit in 6 months

options.label: B
options.text: Do nothing because she denies abuse

options.label: C
options.text: Confront the son in front of her

options.label: D
options.text: Ask the son to explain the bruises and accept his answer

explanation: Report to adult protective services.

Unexplained bruising, weight loss, and fear of a caregiver suggest elder abuse. Physicians in most states are required to report reasonable suspicion; proof is not needed. Interview the patient alone when possible.

vignette: A 3-year-old boy has a spiral fracture of the femur. His mother says he fell off a couch. He also has bruises in different stages of healing on his back.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: C
options.text: Ask the mother's permission to report

options.label: E
options.text: Report only if a skeletal survey shows more fractures

explanation: Report to child protective services.

A spiral fracture in a young child with an implausible story and bruises of different ages strongly suggests abuse. Physicians are mandated reporters, and parental permission is not needed. A skeletal survey is also done.

vignette: A 41-year-old man has had two seizures in the past month despite medication. He drives to work daily and says he cannot afford to stop.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate action?

options.label: A
options.text: Advise him not to drive, document it, and follow state reporting rules

options.label: B
options.text: Increase the dose and say nothing about driving

options.label: D
options.text: Allow him to continue driving if he takes medication

explanation: Advise against driving and follow state law.

Uncontrolled seizures make driving dangerous. The physician must clearly advise the patient not to drive, document it, and follow state rules, which in some states include reporting to the motor vehicle department.

vignette: A 23-year-old woman has vomited repeatedly for 5 days. Blood pressure falls when she stands. Bicarbonate is 38 mEq/L, potassium 2.9 mEq/L, and urine chloride is 8 mEq/L.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.label: B
options.text: IV normal saline with potassium chloride

explanation: Saline with potassium.

Vomiting causes metabolic alkalosis from loss of stomach acid and volume. Low urine chloride (under 20) means the alkalosis is saline-responsive: volume loss makes the kidney hold onto bicarbonate. Saline with potassium chloride corrects it.

vignette: A 40-year-old man has 1 week of severe watery diarrhea. Bicarbonate is 14 mEq/L, chloride 116 mEq/L, and the anion gap is normal.
stem: Which urine anion gap is expected?

options.label: A
options.text: Positive only if potassium is low

explanation: Negative.

In diarrhea, the kidneys respond correctly to acidosis by excreting more ammonium (with chloride), so urine chloride exceeds sodium plus potassium and the urine anion gap is negative. In distal RTA, the kidney cannot excrete acid, and the gap is positive.

vignette: A 32-year-old woman with Sjögren syndrome has kidney stones and muscle weakness. Labs show a non–anion gap metabolic acidosis, potassium of 2.8 mEq/L, and urine pH of 6.5.
stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Distal (type 1) RTA.

The distal tubule cannot secrete acid, so urine pH stays above 5.5 despite acidosis. Low potassium and calcium phosphate stones are typical. Causes include Sjögren syndrome, lupus, and amphotericin B. Treatment is alkali.

vignette: A 66-year-old man with diabetes and mild kidney disease has potassium of 6.0 mEq/L and a mild non–anion gap acidosis. Renin and aldosterone are both low.
stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Type 4 RTA.

Low renin and aldosterone, common in diabetic kidney disease, cause high potassium and mild acidosis. ACE inhibitors, ARBs, NSAIDs, and potassium-sparing diuretics worsen it. Treatment includes a low-potassium diet, loop diuretics, and sometimes fludrocortisone.

vignette: A 70-year-old man with diabetes and an eGFR of 38 mL/min/1.73 m² needs a coronary angiogram.
stem: Which measure best reduces the risk of contrast-induced kidney injury?

options.label: B
options.text: IV isotonic fluid before and after the procedure

explanation: IV isotonic fluid.

Volume expansion with saline or bicarbonate before and after contrast is the main preventive measure in people with reduced kidney function. N-acetylcysteine has not shown clear benefit. The smallest effective contrast dose is used.

vignette: A 45-year-old woman started omeprazole 3 weeks ago. She now has fever, a rash, and creatinine that has risen from 0.8 to 2.4 mg/dL. Urine shows white cells and white cell casts, and urine culture is negative.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate first step?
explanation: Stop the drug.

Acute interstitial nephritis is an allergic reaction in the kidney, most often to proton pump inhibitors, antibiotics (penicillins, cephalosporins), or NSAIDs. Fever, rash, and white cell casts are typical. Stopping the drug is the key step; steroids may help if kidney function does not recover.

vignette: A 72-year-old man with vascular disease starts lisinopril. One week later, creatinine has risen from 1.2 to 2.1 mg/dL. He has an abdominal bruit and recurrent episodes of sudden pulmonary edema.
stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Bilateral renal artery stenosis.

When both renal arteries are narrowed, the kidneys depend on angiotensin II to maintain filtration, so ACE inhibitors cause creatinine to rise sharply. Sudden ("flash") pulmonary edema and an abdominal bruit are clues.

vignette: A 28-year-old woman has new blood pressure of 170/104 mm Hg. She takes no medications and has no family history of hypertension. A bruit is heard over the abdomen. Imaging shows a "string of beads" appearance in the right renal artery.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation: Angioplasty.
Fibromuscular dysplasia causes renovascular hypertension in young women. Unlike atherosclerotic stenosis, it responds well to balloon angioplasty, which often cures the hypertension.

vignette: A 39-year-old man has flank pain, blood in the urine, and hypertension. Both kidneys are enlarged with many cysts. His father died of a brain hemorrhage.
stem: Which complication is he at risk of?
explanation: Berry aneurysm.

Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease is linked to intracranial aneurysms, especially with a family history of brain hemorrhage. Other associations include liver cysts and mitral valve prolapse. Screening MRA is advised for those with a family history.

vignette: A 42-year-old Black man with untreated HIV has heavy proteinuria (9 g/day), edema, and rapidly worsening kidney function.
stem: Which kidney disease is most likely?
explanation: Collapsing FSGS.

HIV-associated nephropathy is a collapsing form of focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, most common in people of African descent with APOL1 risk variants. It causes heavy proteinuria and rapid loss of kidney function. Antiretroviral therapy and ACE inhibitors are the treatment.

vignette: A 22-year-old man has visible blood in his urine 2 days after the start of a sore throat. He has had a similar episode before. Blood pressure and complement levels are normal.
stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: IgA nephropathy.

Visible hematuria within 1–2 days of an upper respiratory infection, often recurring, with normal complement, is typical. It is the most common glomerulonephritis worldwide. Post-streptococcal disease appears weeks later with low C3.

vignette: A 26-year-old man has coughed up blood for 3 days and has dark urine. Creatinine has risen to 4.2 mg/dL over a week. Kidney biopsy shows linear IgG along the glomerular basement membrane.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.label: D
options.text: Plasma exchange with glucocorticoids and cyclophosphamide

explanation: Plasma exchange, steroids, and cyclophosphamide.

Anti-GBM disease (Goodpasture syndrome) attacks type IV collagen in the lungs and kidneys. Linear IgG on biopsy is diagnostic. Plasma exchange removes the antibody while immunosuppression stops its production.

vignette: A 58-year-old woman has had type 1 diabetes for 30 years and now has nephrotic-range proteinuria.
stem: Which finding is expected on kidney biopsy?
explanation: Kimmelstiel–Wilson nodules.

Diabetic nephropathy causes thickening of the glomerular basement membrane, mesangial expansion, and nodular glomerulosclerosis. It is the leading cause of end-stage kidney disease. Spike-and-dome deposits suggest membranous nephropathy.

vignette: A 64-year-old woman with stage 4 chronic kidney disease has hemoglobin of 9.0 g/dL. Ferritin is 40 ng/mL and transferrin saturation is 12%.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate first step?
explanation: Iron first.

Erythropoietin does not work well without adequate iron. In chronic kidney disease, iron is given when ferritin is under about 500 ng/mL and transferrin saturation is under 30%; IV iron is often used. Erythropoietin is started if hemoglobin stays below 10 g/dL.

vignette: A 66-year-old man on hemodialysis has phosphate of 7.4 mg/dL and calcium of 9.6 mg/dL.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.label: E
options.text: Sevelamer with meals and a low-phosphate diet

explanation: Phosphate binder with meals.

High phosphate drives secondary hyperparathyroidism and vascular calcification. Diet restriction and a binder taken with meals, such as sevelamer, lower it. Calcium-based binders are limited when calcium is already high-normal. Calcitriol raises phosphate.

vignette: A 61-year-old man with stage 5 chronic kidney disease is not yet on dialysis.
stem: Which finding is an indication to start dialysis urgently?

options.label: E
options.text: Chest pain with a pericardial friction rub

explanation: Uremic pericarditis.

Urgent dialysis indications are refractory acidosis, refractory high potassium, ingestion of a dialyzable poison, fluid overload not responding to diuretics, and uremic complications such as pericarditis, encephalopathy, or bleeding. A creatinine value alone is not an indication.

vignette: An 86-year-old nursing home resident with dementia is confused and has dry mucous membranes. Sodium is 160 mEq/L. Blood pressure is 124/76 mm Hg and she is not orthostatic.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.label: C
options.text: Rapid correction to 140 mEq/L within 6 hours

options.label: D
options.text: IV 5% dextrose in water, lowering sodium by no more than about 10 mEq/L in 24 hours

explanation: D5W with slow correction.
In a stable patient with high sodium from water loss, free water is replaced slowly to avoid brain swelling. Hypotensive patients get isotonic saline first.

vignette: A 50-year-old man with alcohol use disorder has potassium of 2.6 mEq/L. Despite IV potassium for 2 days, it remains low.
stem: Which test should be checked next?
explanation: Magnesium.
Low magnesium increases potassium loss in the kidney, and potassium cannot be corrected until magnesium is replaced. Low magnesium is common with alcohol use, diarrhea, and diuretics.

vignette: A 55-year-old man with uncontrolled diabetes has sodium of 128 mEq/L and glucose of 640 mg/dL. Serum osmolality is high.
stem: Which of the following is the best explanation for the low sodium?

options.label: D
options.text: Water drawn out of cells by high glucose

explanation: Water drawn out of cells.
High glucose raises serum osmolality and pulls water from cells, diluting sodium. Sodium falls by about 1.6–2.4 mEq/L for every 100 mg/dL rise in glucose. Treating the glucose corrects the sodium.

vignette: A 46-year-old man with nephrotic syndrome from membranous nephropathy develops sudden left flank pain, visible blood in the urine, and a rise in creatinine.
stem: Which of the following is the most likely cause?
explanation: Renal vein thrombosis.

Nephrotic syndrome causes a clotting tendency from urinary loss of anticoagulant proteins such as antithrombin III. Membranous nephropathy carries the highest risk of renal vein thrombosis. Anticoagulation is the treatment.

vignette: A 26-year-old man of Mediterranean descent has hemoglobin of 11.8 g/dL, MCV 63 fL, a high red cell count, and normal ferritin.
stem: Which test is most appropriate?
explanation: Hemoglobin electrophoresis.

Very small red cells with mild anemia, a high red cell count, and normal iron stores suggest thalassemia trait (Mentzer index, MCV divided by red cell count, under 13). Electrophoresis shows raised HbA2 in beta-thalassemia trait; alpha-thalassemia trait may need genetic testing.

vignette: A 66-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis has hemoglobin of 10.2 g/dL and MCV 82 fL.
stem: Which set of iron studies is expected?

options.label: A
options.text: Low iron, high TIBC, low ferritin

options.label: B
options.text: High iron, high TIBC, low ferritin

options.label: C
options.text: Normal iron, normal TIBC, low ferritin

options.label: D
options.text: High iron, low TIBC, high ferritin

options.label: E
options.text: Low iron, low TIBC, normal or high ferritin

explanation: Low iron, low TIBC, normal or high ferritin.
In anemia of chronic disease, hepcidin traps iron in storage. Serum iron is low, but transferrin (TIBC) is low and ferritin is normal or high. Iron deficiency has high TIBC and low ferritin.

vignette: A 24-year-old man of African descent develops dark urine and jaundice 2 days after starting trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. The blood film shows red cells with bites taken out of them and inclusions on special staining.
stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: G6PD deficiency.

Oxidizing drugs (sulfonamides, primaquine, dapsone), fava beans, or infection trigger hemolysis. Heinz bodies are denatured hemoglobin, and macrophages remove them, leaving bite cells. The level can be falsely normal during an attack, so testing is repeated later.

vignette: A 14-year-old girl has fatigue, mild jaundice, and an enlarged spleen. Her father had his spleen removed. Hemoglobin is 10.1 g/dL, MCHC is high, and the direct antiglobulin test is negative.
stem: Which test best confirms the diagnosis?
explanation: EMA binding test.

Hereditary spherocytosis comes from defects in red cell membrane proteins such as spectrin and ankyrin. It causes spherocytes, high MCHC, a negative antiglobulin test, splenomegaly, and gallstones. Flow cytometry for eosin-5-maleimide binding is the preferred test.

vignette: A 58-year-old woman with lupus has fatigue and jaundice. Hemoglobin is 7.9 g/dL, reticulocytes are high, and the blood film shows spherocytes. Direct antiglobulin test is positive for IgG.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation: Glucocorticoids.
Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia (IgG antibodies, often with lupus, lymphoma, or drugs) is treated first with steroids. Rituximab or splenectomy is used if it does not respond.

vignette: A 64-year-old man with septic shock has oozing from IV sites. Platelets are 42,000/mm³, PT and PTT are prolonged, fibrinogen is low, and D-dimer is very high.
stem: Which of the following is the most important treatment?
explanation: Treat the cause.

Disseminated intravascular coagulation uses up clotting factors and platelets. Treating the underlying cause, here sepsis, is the key step. Platelets, plasma, or cryoprecipitate are given for bleeding or before procedures.

vignette: A 19-year-old woman has heavy periods since they started and frequent nosebleeds. Her mother has similar problems. Platelet count is normal and PTT is slightly prolonged.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment before a dental extraction?
explanation: Desmopressin.

Von Willebrand disease is the most common inherited bleeding disorder and causes mucosal bleeding. Desmopressin releases von Willebrand factor stored in blood vessel walls and works in most cases of type 1. Tranexamic acid helps for dental work.

vignette: A 4-year-old boy has a swollen, painful knee after a minor fall. His maternal uncle has a bleeding disorder. PTT is prolonged and corrects when mixed with normal plasma; PT and platelets are normal.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation: Factor VIII concentrate.

Hemophilia A is X-linked, so boys are affected through their mothers' families. Bleeding into joints is typical. PTT is prolonged and corrects with mixing (a missing factor, not an inhibitor). Hemophilia B (factor IX) looks the same and is distinguished by factor assays.

vignette: A 72-year-old man taking warfarin for atrial fibrillation has an INR of 9.2. He has no bleeding.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.text: IV vitamin K and prothrombin complex concentrate

options.label: B
options.text: Continue warfarin at the same dose

options.label: D
options.text: Hold warfarin and give oral vitamin K

explanation: Hold warfarin and give oral vitamin K.

For an INR above 10 without bleeding, warfarin is held and oral vitamin K is given; between 4.5 and 10 without bleeding, holding warfarin is usually enough. IV vitamin K and factor concentrates are for serious bleeding.

vignette: A 70-year-old woman taking warfarin has a large brain hemorrhage on CT. INR is 3.4.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.label: A
options.text: Four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate and IV vitamin K

explanation: Prothrombin complex and IV vitamin K.

Life-threatening bleeding on warfarin needs immediate reversal. Four-factor PCC replaces factors II, VII, IX, and X within minutes, and IV vitamin K keeps the reversal going. Protamine reverses heparin; idarucizumab reverses dabigatran.

vignette: A 62-year-old man has itching after hot showers, headaches, and burning pain in his feet. Hemoglobin is 19.6 g/dL and the spleen is enlarged. A JAK2 mutation is present.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?
explanation: Phlebotomy and aspirin.

Polycythemia vera is a JAK2-driven bone marrow disorder. Phlebotomy to a hematocrit below 45% and low-dose aspirin reduce clotting. Hydroxyurea is added for patients at high risk, such as those over 60 or with prior clots.

vignette: Ten minutes into a red cell transfusion, a 45-year-old woman develops fever, chills, low back pain, and red urine. Blood pressure falls.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate first step?
explanation: Stop the transfusion.

Fever, back pain, red urine, and low blood pressure early in a transfusion suggest acute hemolysis from ABO incompatibility. Stop at once, keep the IV open with saline, recheck patient and blood unit identity, and send samples to the blood bank.

vignette: A 79-year-old man is dying of pancreatic cancer. For the past few hours his breathing has been noisy and gurgling. He appears comfortable, but his family is distressed.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.text: Glycopyrrolate and reassurance for the family

explanation: Glycopyrrolate and reassurance.

"Death rattle" is caused by secretions the dying patient can no longer clear and is usually not distressing to the patient. Positioning, anticholinergic drugs, and explaining it to the family help. Deep suctioning is uncomfortable and rarely helps.

vignette: A 75-year-old woman with metastatic lung cancer in hospice becomes agitated, confused, and is seeing things that are not there. Reversible causes have been addressed.
stem: Which medication is most appropriate?
explanation: Haloperidol.

Haloperidol is first-line for delirium at the end of life. Benzodiazepines alone can worsen delirium but may be added for severe agitation. Anticholinergic drugs such as diphenhydramine also worsen confusion.

vignette: A 68-year-old man with cancer takes 60 mg of oral morphine a day with good pain control. He can no longer swallow.
stem: Which daily dose of IV morphine is equivalent?
explanation: 20 mg.

Oral morphine is about one-third as potent as IV morphine because of first-pass metabolism in the liver, so 60 mg orally is about 20 mg IV. When switching between different opioids, the dose is reduced further for incomplete cross-tolerance.

vignette: A 72-year-old woman with metastatic cancer and worsening kidney failure takes morphine for pain. She now has muscle jerks, confusion, and drowsiness.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate change?
explanation: Switch to fentanyl.

Morphine's active metabolites build up in kidney failure and cause myoclonus, confusion, and sedation. Fentanyl and methadone are safer in kidney failure. Codeine and tramadol also have metabolites that accumulate.

vignette: A 64-year-old man with prostate cancer has severe pain from a single bone metastasis in his hip despite opioids and NSAIDs. There is no fracture.
stem: Which of the following is the most effective additional treatment?
explanation: Radiation therapy.
External beam radiation, often as a single dose, relieves pain from a bone metastasis in most patients within weeks. Bisphosphonates or denosumab reduce future skeletal events.

vignette: A 66-year-old woman with advanced ovarian cancer has bowel obstruction from widespread tumor and is not a surgical candidate. She has nausea, vomiting, and cramping.
stem: Which medication best reduces her symptoms?
explanation: Octreotide.

Octreotide reduces gut secretions, decreasing vomiting and distension in malignant bowel obstruction. Antiemetics such as haloperidol, steroids, and a venting gastrostomy tube may also help. Prokinetics like metoclopramide are avoided in complete obstruction.

vignette: A 73-year-old woman whose husband died 2 months ago is sad, sometimes hears his voice calling her, and has trouble sleeping. She still sees friends, cooks, and looks after her garden, and she does not feel worthless or want to die.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.text: Support and reassurance that this is normal grief

options.label: E
options.text: Start a benzodiazepine for sleep every night

explanation: Normal grief.

Sadness, poor sleep, and even briefly hearing or sensing the dead person are common in normal grief. She is still functioning and has no feelings of worthlessness or suicidal thoughts. Support and follow-up are appropriate; prolonged grief disorder is considered after a year.

vignette: A 58-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer is receiving chemotherapy and wants to continue it. She has pain, nausea, and anxiety.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: C
options.text: Refer to hospice, which requires stopping chemotherapy

options.label: D
options.text: Palliative care consultation alongside her cancer treatment

options.label: E
options.text: Wait until she stops chemotherapy before addressing symptoms

explanation: Palliative care alongside treatment.

Palliative care treats symptoms and supports patients at any stage, together with cancer treatment, and improves quality of life. Hospice is a specific form of palliative care for the last months of life, when the patient chooses to stop disease-directed treatment.

vignette: A 25-year-old woman had a normal Pap smear 3 years ago. She has no symptoms and is sexually active.
stem: Which cervical cancer screening is recommended now?
explanation: Pap smear.

For ages 21–29, cervical cytology every 3 years is recommended; HPV testing is not used alone in this age group because HPV infection is common and usually clears. From 30–65, options include HPV testing every 5 years or cytology every 3 years.

vignette: A 46-year-old woman at average risk asks about breast cancer screening. She has never had a mammogram.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation?
explanation: Mammography every 2 years.
Current US Preventive Services Task Force guidance recommends screening mammography every 2 years for average-risk women aged 40–74. MRI is for women at high risk, such as BRCA carriers.

vignette: A 35-year-old woman's mother had ovarian cancer at 52, and her maternal aunt had breast cancer at 41. She has no symptoms.
stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: Genetic counseling.

Early-onset breast cancer and ovarian cancer in close relatives suggest a hereditary syndrome such as BRCA1 or BRCA2. Counseling decides whether genetic testing is appropriate and explains what positive results would mean for screening and prevention.

vignette: A 51-year-old woman has HER2-positive breast cancer. Trastuzumab is planned.
stem: Which test should be done before starting it?
explanation: Echocardiogram.
Trastuzumab can weaken the heart muscle, usually reversibly. Ejection fraction is measured before starting and every 3 months during treatment. The risk is higher with anthracyclines.

vignette: A 45-year-old premenopausal woman is taking tamoxifen after treatment for estrogen receptor–positive breast cancer.
stem: Which risk is increased?
explanation: Endometrial cancer.

Tamoxifen blocks estrogen in the breast but stimulates the endometrium, raising the risk of endometrial cancer, as well as blood clots and stroke. It protects bone. Abnormal vaginal bleeding on tamoxifen needs evaluation.

vignette: A 63-year-old postmenopausal woman is starting anastrozole for estrogen receptor–positive breast cancer.
stem: Which test should be done at baseline?
explanation: Bone density scan.
